Expansion of coal industry 
†613. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: 
SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
Will the Minister of COAL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Planning Commission has given some 
suggestions for expansion of the coal industry as per the requirement of 
the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the decisions taken by Government to implement these suggestions? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL (DR. DASARI 
NARAYANA RAO): (a) to (c) Yes, Si r. The Planning Commission has 
suggested some critical initiatives for the development of coal sector which, 
inter alia, include the following: 
(i) Expedite passing of Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Amendment Bill, 
2000 which would permit private sector in non-captive mining in 
order to augment domestic coal production for meeting the rising 
coal demand.. 
†Original notice of the Question was received in Hindi. 
215 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005] 
(ii) Amend the provisions of Mines & Minerals Development and 
Regulation (MMDR)Act, 1957 to facilitate offering of coal blocks 
to potential enterpreneurs on competitive bidding basis. 
(iii) Enlarge the scope of captive mining by permitting captive block 
holders to sell incidental coal production during development of 
the block at least to Coal India Ltd. (CIL). 
(iv) Restructure Coal India Ltd. (CIL) by doing away with the holding 
company structure and extending autonomy to individual coal 
producing companies for promot ing competition amongst the 
national coal companies. 
(v) Permit trading of coal by remo ving it from the list of essential 
commodities. 
(vi) Change grading and pricing of non-coking coal from the existing 
Useful Heat Value (UHV) to Gross Calorific Value (GCV) to 
encourage efficient use and allocation and promote use of washed 
coal. 
(vii) Amend the provisions of Contract Labour (Regulation & Abolition) 
Act, 1970 to facilitate offloading of certain activities in coal mining 
for improved economics of operations. 
(viii) As a step towards abolishing coal linkages these linkages may 
be made tradable by power plants. 
The decisions/actions taken by the Government in respect of the above 
suggestions of the Planning Commission areas under:— 
(i) The Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Amendment Bill, 2000 has been 
introduced in Rajya Sabha in April, 2000 to permit private 
participation in non-captive coal mining in order to augment coal 
production in the country. 
(ii) An amendment to the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 has 
been proposed for allocation of coal blocks on competitive bidding 
basis and for that a Cabinet Note has been prepared. 
(iii) As regards enlarging the scope of captive mining by permitting 
captive holders to sell incidental coal production during the 
development of a mine to CIL, this has already been decided by 
the Government.

India Limited, the Government has decided to delegate powers 
exercised by CIL relating to pr ocurement of all items except

decided to completely delegate power relatiang to marketing in

NARAYANA RAO): (a) and (b) As reported by Coal India Limited, prior to 
†Original notice of the Question was received in Hindi.

nationalization there were 70 mine fire s in Jharia coalfield, which are 
presently under the jurisdiction of Bharat Coking Coal Limited (BCCL). As 
a result of the efforts made by BCCL 10 fires have been extinguished and

jurisdiction of Bharat Coking Coal Limited. 
(c) Presently there are no other mines of Coal India Ltd. having active

which have been controlled and sealed off. It is not possible to make an 
yearly assessment of coal getting de stroyed by fires. However, as per 
study conducted by Central Mine Plan ning & Design Institute Limited 
reserves of coal lost due to fire is estimated at around 37 million tonnes in 
Jharia Coalfield. 
(d) The following steps have been taken to control/extinguish fire in coal 
mines: 
(i) Sand flushing into active fire zone from surface to under ground 
through boreholes. 
(ii) Surface blanketing to prevent breathing in of air to the fire area. 
(iii) Inert gas flushing from surface through boreholes to extinguish 
fire. 
(iv) Quenching of spot fire and mining out the quenched coal. 
(v) Sealing of the part of the mine under fire by construction of the fire 
stoppings/isolation stoppings. 
(vi) Application of fire resistant sealant in and around the isolation 
stoppings/fire stoppings. 
(vii) Regular monitoring with the help of Co-detectors, toximeter, air 
sampling and analysis of the same at colliery level. 
(viii) Trench cutting by mechanized means to excavate fire and to 
prevent spread of the same. 
(ix) Intentional flooding by water to quench the fire in some mines. 
Apart from above action, 16 schemes for dealing with fires and control 
of subsidence have been sanctioned and funded by the Government. Out 
of these, 8 schemes have been completed. A Master Plan has also been 
prepared to deal with fires and control of subsidence in Jharia coalfields as 
a long term measure.

Departments for improving the road, rail and air connectivity, tele-
communication network and media coverage in the North-Eastern Region

(i) Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has proposed to

 has received ADB assistance for commencing a study of the

†654. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: W ill the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:

reforms in the existing education system, for providing excellent training

DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M.A.A. FATMI): (a) to (c) The education system 
in the country is guided by the Na tional Policy on Education, 1986 (as 
modified in 1992) which, among other things, envisages that effective 
measures will be taken in the dire ction of the common school system. 
The Policy also envisages overhauling of the system of teacher education 
in the country with emphasis on continuing education and the need for 
teachers to meet the thrusts envisaged in the policy.

Central Advisory Board of Education has been constituted on 8.9.2004 
under the Chairmanship of Shri Tarun Gogoi, Chief Minister of Assam on 
the subject of 'Girls Education and the common school system'. The 
National Council for Teacher Education, a statutory body, is responsible 
for regulation and the proper observance of norms and standards in teacher 
education at the Elementary and Secondary levels. The revised Teacher 
Education Scheme for the Tenth Plan period envisages establishment of 
one District Institute of Education and Training (DIETV District Resource 
Centre (DRC) in every District and making them optimally functional and 
operational or improving the quality of programmes undertaken by them 
especially those of pre-service and in -service training so as to enable 
them to effectively play their nodal role in improving quality of Education, 
as measured in terms of levels of learner achievement.

Illiteracy 
†655. PROF. MM. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that as on date more than 36 crore persons are 
illiterate in the country; 
(b) whether Government have formulated any time-bound programme in 
this regard; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the effective steps being taken by Government to increase the literacy 
rate as well as to educate the illiterate people? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M.A.A. FATMI): (a) As per Census 2001, there 
were 30.41 crore non-literates in 7+age-group in the country. 
(b) to (d) In the Elementary Education Sector, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan 
(SSA) has been launched with a holis tic and convergent approach, to 
implement Universalisation of Elementary Education in a mission mode 
with district focus. The goals of SSA are: 
• All children in School, Education Guarantee Centre, Alternate School, 
'Back-to-School' camp by 2003. 
• All children complete five years of primary schooling by 2007. 
• All children complete eight years of elementary schooling by 2010. 
• Focus on elementary education of satisfactory quality with emphasis 
on education for life. 
• Bridge all gender and social category gaps at primary stage by 
2007 and at elementary education level by 2010. 
• Universal retention by 2010. 
The National Literacy Mission (NLM) aims to provide functional literacy 
to non-literates in 15-35 age group. The target of NLM is to attain a 
sustainable threshold literacy rate of  75% of 2007. The thrust areas of 
NLM are improving female literacy in low female literacy areas, to organize 
residual illiteracy projects in areas,  which have substantial number of 
illiterates, and to set up continuing education centre s for providing 
opportunities for life long learning to the neo-literates.

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005] 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that earlier also the question papers of the CAT 
were found to be available in the market several times well before the

(d) the steps being taken by Government to retain the falling goodwill of 
these most prestigious and inter nationally acclaimed management 
institutions and prevent the reoccurrence of such misdeeds? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M.A.A FATMI): (a) and (b) Astatement is attached 
(see below). 
(c) and (d) The Common Admission Test (CAT) for entry to all Indian 
Institutes of Management (IIMs) and some other Management Institutions 
conducted on November 23, 2003 had to be cancelled due to alleged 
leakage of question paper. The test was successfully re-conducted on 
February 15, 2004. The entire procedure was thoroughly reviewed in a 
combined meeting of the IIMs. As a result several additional precautions 
i.e. change of the printing press, additional seal for each question paper, 
additional security during test construction, additional deployment of faculty 
and staff during conduction of the test etc. were implemented in subsequent 
tests. 
Statement 
Leakage of results of CAT Examinations 
As per the report received from the Indian Institute of Management, 
Ahmedabad (IIMA), CAT 2004 was conducted on November 21, 2004. 
Answer sheets were scanned by each of the institutes immediately after 
that. On December 1, the admissi on chairmen of all the IIMs and the 
Common Admission Test (CAT) center coordinators met at CAT Center to 
do all necessary checks for processing  of the results. The final CDs 
containing the scores and the confirmed complete addresses were sent 
to all the IIMs and to the scorecard-printing agency on December 15, 
2004. 
The CAT group decided internally that by midnight December 21/22, 
2004, the results would be displayed on the websites of all IIMs and that 
posting of the scorecards would also start simultaneously. This was an 
internal decision, and there was no public announcement about this date. 
Before displaying the scorecards on their respective websites, each 
284 

[9 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
institute goes through a process of te sting from the view point of easy 
accessibility prior to uploading on to the website. The testing for the IIMA 
website was done in the evening of December 20, and early morning of 
December 21, 2004. Since comprehensive process of testing requires 
uploading and testing on-line, it is possible that some candidates may 
have got access to the link by mere coincidence. As the whole operation 
is to be in the public domain in any case, such coincidences would be 
inconsequential in terms of the ultimate outcome. Moreover, only the 
individuals who furnish the respective Test Registration Number and Date 
of Birth can have access to their scorecard. 
The results are actually declared through the printed scorecard sent by 
registered post to every candidate who took the test and the printed 
scorecard is the only valid document showing the result. In the CAT 2004 
Bulletin issued in July 2004, it was clearly indicated that all eligible test 
takers would receive their scorecards by the end of December, 2004. 
However, to facilitate faster accessibility of results from the viewpoint of 
the candidates, CAT Group also decided to allow candidates to have access 
to the electronic version of their scorecards. This was done primarily with 
the objective of providing better service to the test takers. The exercise of 
prior testing was meant to ensure a smooth and trouble free access to 
everyone. 
As decided by the CAT Group, the results of CAT 2004 were placed on 
the website of each IIM by midnight of December 21/22, 2004.

Traffic (Prevention) Act 1956 is being made more stringent for traffickers,

activities include awareness campaign through TV. and Radio, sensitization 
of police and lower judiciary and involvement of NGOs in prevention and 
rescue activities.

Preparation of annual report by Prasar Bharati 
693. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of INFORMATION 
AND BROADCATING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that even after seven years of its existence, 
Prasar Bharati has not prepared even a single Annual Report; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that preparation of Annual Report is mandatory 
under the Prasar Bharati Act; and 
(c) if so, the reasons for not preparing the Annual Reports? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCATING (SHRI S. 
JAIPAL REDDY): (a) to (c) Section 32(2)(k) of Prasar Bharati Act stipulates 
that the Central Government may by notification, make rules, which may 
provide the form in which and the time within which, the Corporation shall 
prepare their Annual Report under Section 31 of the said Act. The 
Government on 18th May, 2004, notified the rules in this regard, which are 
known as Prasar Bharati (Broadcasting Corporation of India), Annual Report 
of the Corporation Rules, 2004. Prasar Bharati has set in motion the process 
of preparation of Annual Report as required under the Prasar Bharati. Act. 
Prior to issuance of these rules, the information pertaining to the Prasar 
Bharati has been incorporated in the Annual Report of the Ministry of 
Information & Broadcasting.

694. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND 
BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that Geetakrishnan Committee on 
Expenditure Reforms had recommended that DAVP should be wound up; 
(b) if so, what is Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) when the existing guidelines relating to advertisement policy were framed; 
(d) whether views of the newspaper industry were taken into consideration 
at that point of time; and 
(e) as these guidelines are required to be revised urgently in consultation 
with the newspaper industry by when Governement propose to do that? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. 
JAIPAL REDDY): (a) The Geetakrishnan Committee on Expenditure 
312

Reforms had recommended that the ac tivities of the Directorate of 
Advertising & Visual Publicity (DAVP) including release of advertisements, 
could be decentralised and left to the individual Ministries/Departments 
and DAVP should concern itself with establishment of rate contracts relating 
to advertisements to be followed by various Ministries. 
(b) The Government is of the view that if the activities of DAVP are 
decentralised, the Ministries/Departments could need more staff than that 
with DAVP at present and thereby defeat the very purpose of economy in 
Government. DAVP has been providing facilities at single point with various 
inputs including plan, design, language versions, multi-media requirements

Statement 
Monitoring of EPICs 
The Election Commission of India is directly responsible for the 
implementation and monitoring of the scheme of Elector's Photo Identity 
Cards (EPICs). An extract of information received from the Commission in 
the matter is given below:— 
"The Commission had received some complaints regarding persons 
possessing Electroral Photo Identity Cards (EPIC) who could not caste 
their vote during the General Elections to Lok Sabha and State Legislative 
Assemblies of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Orissa and Sikkim conducted 
in April-May, 2004, as their names were missing from the electoral rolls 
used for the conduct of these elections. The Commission had forwarded 
all complaints received by it to the Chief Electoral Officers concerned for 
appropriate action to restore the ent ries and to ascertain the reasons 
behind the missing names. 
The general elections to the State Legislative Assemblies of Arunachal 
Pradesh and Maharashtra were due to be held in September-October, 
2004. No complaints were received during the general election to Lok 
Sabha in Arunachal Pradesh about omission of names of persons 
possessing Electroral Photo Identity Cards (EPIC). However, there were 
some such complaints received from the State of Maharashtra. Therefore, 
the Commission ordered another special summary revision in the entire 
State of Maharashtra with the same qualifying date, i.e. 1.1.2004 before 
the General Elections to the State Legislative Assembly to give on 
opportunity to all the persons possessing EPIC whose names were missing 
as well as other eligible persons to get their names enrolled. The 
programme of special summary revision commenced with draft publication 
of rolls on 15.6.2004 and the final publication was made on 18.8.2004. 
The Chief Election Commissioner in the Press Conference held on 24th 
August, 2004 for announeing the programme of general elections to the 
330 

[9 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Legislative Assemblies of Arunachal Pradesh and Maharashtra and bye-
elections to various vacancies to Lok Sabha/Legislative Assemblies had 
also made repeated appeal to the eligible citizens to check the electoral 
roll to ensure that their names were included and point out omissions, if 
any, within the period available as per law. 
During the general elections to Arunachal Pradesh and Maharashtra 
Legislative Assembly held in October, 2004 there were no complaints about 
omission of names of any eligible person, including those having- EPICs 
from the electoral roll. 
In respect of all States and UTs, except Arunachal Pradesh and 
Maharashtra, the Commission has ordered revision of electoral rolls with 
respect to 01.01.2005 as the qualifying date to give an opportunity to all 
the persons possessing EPIC whose names were found missing at the 
time of general election to Lok Sabha as well as other eligible persons to 
get their names enrolled in the electoral roll and delete names of dead and 
shifted electors. In the States of Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, 
Nagaland, Tripura and Jammu & Kashmir, the nature of revision ordered 
was intensive, i.e. by way of house-to-house enumeration. In rest of the 
States, except Tamil Nadu, the revision ordered was special summary, 
i.e., the existing rolls of 2004 were published in draft for inviting claims and 
objections from the eligible persons. 
In Tamil Nadu, in 38 Assembly Constituencies wholly or partly covered 
in Municipal Corporation areas of Chennai, Salem, Coimbatore, 
Timchirappali, Madurai, and Tiruneiveli, a special revision of intensive nature 
with house-to-house enumeration will be carried out with 1.1.2005 as the 
qualifying date. In the remaining 196 Assembly Constituencies of the State 
a special revision of summary nature will be undertaken with 1.1.2005 as 
the qualifying date. 
In the State of Arunachal Pradesh an intensive revision is contemplated 
and in Maharashtra, a special summary revision will be undertaken. The 
programme of revision with 01.01.2005 as the qualifying date is yet to be 
finalized in both the States. 
In the comprehensive guidelines issued by the Commission for the 
revision of rolls with respect to 1.1.2005 as the qualifying date it has been 
specifically mentioned that befor e deletion of any name of person 
possessing EPIC, either not f ound residing during house-to-house 
enumeration during intensive revision or while disposing of objections to 
such inclusions filed in Form-7 appended to the Registration of Electors 
331 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005] 
Rules, 1960 during summary revision, a re-verification shall be made to 
ensure that no names are wrongly deleted. It has been further instructed 
that list of such electors can even be given to the political parties or 
published if deemed necessary. These steps are aimed to ensure that 
names of eligible persons especially those possessing EPIC are not deleted 
without valid reason. 
It may be added that holding an EPIC is not an authority to vote, as the 
right to vote is based on the existence of the name of the person in the 
electoral roll being used for the election from the constituency where he/ 
she ordinarily resides."

332 

[9 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA

thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW AND JUSTICE 
(SHRI K. VENKATAPATHY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) A study sponsored by the National Commission for Women 
on coparcenary rights of women in Andhra Pradesh was conducted by 
NALSAR, University of Law, Hyderabad. The project report submitted by 
NALSAR to the National Commission for Women, inter alia, contains the 
following suggestions:— 
"(i) The coparcenary should be done away with in Hindu Succession 
Act, 1956 as we have in 1956 done away with Stridhana. 
(ii) Equal share to daughter along with son in the ancestral property 
should be done on the lines of Section 8 of the Hindu succession 
Act, 1956, which confers equal share in self-acquired property. 
(iii) The right to claim partition should be given to daughter along with 
sons and predeceased son's wife/widow. 
(iv) The members of Joint Hindu Family can still continue and those 
of them who wish to stay toget her can stay as co-owners of 
property." 
The Law Commission of India, a fter studying the various State 
amendments to the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 including the Hindu 
Succession (Andhra Pradesh Amendment) Act, 1986 and the Kerala Joint 
Hindu Family System (Abolition) Act, 1975 submitted its 174th Report on 
"Property Rights of Women : Proposed Reforms under the Hindu Law" to 
the Central Government. With a view to implementing the said Report of 
the Commission and after consulting the State Governments, the Hindu 
Succession (Amendment) Bill, 2004 was introduced in the Rajya Sabha 
on the 20th December, 2004. The Bill is currently under examination of the 
Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, 
Public Grievances, Law and Justice.

budget estimate of Rs192.37 crores and Rs. 186.25 crores allocated for 
the year 2002-03 and 2003-04, respectively. Full utilization of allocated 
funds depends on various factor viz. the timely submission of inspection 
reports, recommendations of the State Govemments/UT Administrations, 
receipt of utilization certificates from the non-governmental organizations 
receiving grants etc.

statutory authority having powers under the Persons with Disabilities Act,

Reservation for disabled 
737. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE AND 
EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any clear cut policy of reservations in civil services 
and educational institution for disabled; 
(b) if so, the details therefor; 
(c) the case of non-implementation of reservation policy for disabled; 
and 
(d) the action taken by Government to ensure compliance of the 
reservation policy? 
THE MINISTER OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT 
(SHRIMATI MEIRA KUMAR): (a) and (b) Yes Sir. Section 33 of the Persons 
with Disabilities Act, 1995 provides that every appropriate Government 
shall provide for reservation of not less than 3% of vacancies in identified 
posts in every establishment for perso ns with disabilities of which one 
percent each shall be reserved for persons suffering form (i) blindness or 
low vision; (ii) hearing impairment and (iii) locomotor disability or cerebral 
palsy. 
Section 39 of the Act stipulates that all Government educational 
institutions and other educational in stitutions receiving aid from the

labour for construction of socially and economically useful public assets.

micro/group enterprises and to impart skill training to 5,00,000 persons have been

DR. P.C. ALEXANDER (Maharashtra): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I rise 
to move the two amendments for which I had given notice and I wish to focus 
only on the two problems which I have mentioned in my notice. The first is the 
failure on the part of the President's Address to make mention about the need 
and importance of comprehensive statutor y reforms to improve the working of 
political parties in our country and the second is the failure to mention the 
need for a total restructuring of the educ ational system to serve certain wider 
objectives mentioned in the Preamble of  the Constitution, particularly for 
promoting national integration and unity. 
If we look at the last 58 years of our Independence and our 
experiments in the working of  the parliamentary system of democracy, we will 
have to admit honestly that we had not come up to the expectations which 
were made in the framing of the Constitution by the founding fathers of our 
Republic. Actually, if we make an assessment on the performance of our 
country for 58 years of the working of  the parliamentary system, we will have 
to admit that we have not done well. But still we are persisting with that system 
hoping that we will improve as years go by. If you ask me honestly to give my 
assessment as to where we have failed in making a success of the system, I 
will have absolutely no hesitation in putting my finger on the poor working of 
the political parties in our country. In  my judgement, this is the number one 
reason why the parliamentary system has not succeeded to the extent it 
should have in our country. It is the basic condition of the parliamentary 
democracy that it is successful only if there is the pr emise of a sound 
parliamentary system. If we look at wh at we have achieved over the last 58 
years, we will say with great regret that we have not succeeded in evolving 
healthy national parties. In a huge sub- continent like ours with over a billion 
people, we still have Governments run by national parties but with the help of 
a large multiplicity of small parties. If we look at the State Governments also, 
we will find that the State parties them selves do not have the real strength to 
run the Government and they 
461 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005]  
are in turn dependent on small parties. I consider it a very serious threat to the 
future of parliamentary democracy in our country. Sir, if we look back when the 
Congress Party contested elections after three years of Independence, i.e. in 
1952, there were 74 small parties contesting the elections along with the 
Congress Party. But the Congress Party won 364 seats out of 489 seats. By 
1957, the number of parties was betw een 80 and 90 and the Congress Party 
won 371 seats out of 493. In  1952, the second largest party in Parliament next 
to the Congress Party which had 364 seats, had only 12 Members. In 1957, 
the second largest party had only 19 Members. Just think of the situation 
today. After the 1999 elections, the two major national parties, i.e. the 
Congress Party and the BJP have really performed miserably, if I may use this 
word. The party which is running the Government today or leading the coalition 
today, has just 145 Members on its own and the single largest Opposition 
Party today has just 138 Members in a House of 540 Members. In a 
parliamentary democracy, the ruling party whether it leads the coalition or runs 
the Government, should be somewhere near the half way mark and if it does 
not depend on others, it should certainl y have more than the half way mark. 
The opposition party which is claiming to run the Government by defeating the 
party in power, should be near that mark. 
But these two great national parties have declined and they are on 
the road to decline for various reasons which I want to mention before you. Sir, 
I have 10 minutes only according to the time that you have allotted me... 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA): Twelve 
minutes. 
DR. P.C. ALEXANDER: Therefore, I will rush through them. I, in my 
analysis, have identified seven major reasons as to why the national parties, 
including the Congress (I) and the BJP, have declined over the last 10 years. 
    
The first reason, in my opinion, is absence of inner party democracy. I 
am sorry to use this word; nomination cu lture has become the rule of political 
parties in our country. The only excepti on I would say is the Communist Party; 
I am not a great admirer of the Communist Party (Marxist), but all credit to 
them because I read with great interest from newspapers about Kerala where 
elections were held at the district level;  then elections were held at the State 
level, and then the State Party's 
462 

[9 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA  
Secretariat emerged as a result of elec tions at all the levels necessary. But 
what we see with other political parties , not only the big political parties, the 
national parties, but also other State parties,  is that it is all nomination culture 
there. They meet at the headquarters whether in Delhi or Lucknow or Patna, 
wherever these may be, and a few pe ople sit together and decide who should 
be the members of the Working Commi ttee, who should be the CPCC 
President or the State Party President and who should be the nominee for 
elections to this post or that post. This is the negation of democracy. If we 
believe in democratic principles, we should practise it in our own party. But 
because we do not allow inner party democracy, we find the national parties 
today at the beck and call of small pa rties which have a strength of two or 
three or, as in Kerala, there is even a one-member party. 
The second major reason out of the seven which I have identified is, 
erosion of accountability in  these parties. We talk of accountability of the 
Government to Parliament. But where is the accountability of the leaders of 
the parties to their parties' organisat ions? When an MP or an MLA is elected, 
because he had been nominated to be a candidate from a particular 
constituency, not by the members of the party in that constituency but by the 
High Commands sitting in New Delhi, Patna or Lucknow, how can he be 
accountable to the members in the constituency? He is accountable to his 
High Command; otherwise he will not get nominated for the second time. It is 
a very dangerous practice that we ar e following. Mr. Deputy Chairman, this 
never happens in an advanced democracy. I am a very close student of the 
Parliamentary system in the United Kingdom, and I can say from my own 
personal observation that no Prime Minister, no party leader, will ever think of 
telling the Constituency, "So and so is going to be your candidate. You vote for 
him." The Constituency alone has the right to elect or select a person who is to 
be their candidate. 
The third reason is -- I am using a strong term -- the so-called High 
Commands of parties stifling leadership at the local levels. This is a new 
development. It never happened in Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru's long period of 
time. In Nehru's time, the High Command depended upon strong leaders at 
the State level. Today the leaders at th e State level cannot be qualified as 
strong, and they are totally dependent on their existence; they are at the beck 
and call of the people sitting in these Headquarters. Think of the days when 
Shri Kamaraj was the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu from 1954 to 1965 -- 11 
long years and nobody disturbed him.   Dr. B.C. Roy was 
463 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005]  
the Chief Minister of Bengal from 1948 to 1962. Govind Vallabh Pant remained 
Chief Minister from 1946 to 1965. Shri Pratap Singh Kairon remained Chief 
Minister from 1956-64. These were th e tall stalwarts who strengthened the 
national parties. The national party leaders derived strength from these 
stalwarts unlike today where the local leaders are waiting for the orders and 
diktats from the Headquarters. 
My fourth reason is 'consciously allowing groupism in party 
organisations in States'. I say 'consciously' because -- I am sorry again to 
make a very strong statement -- people who control the party at the top do not 
like strong partymen at the State level. So, they allow groups to fight against 
each other; they cancel their strength; and all groups depend upon the Centre. 
The fifth point is about defections from one party to another. An 
honest attempt is being made to prevent defections. But we are seeing 
devious ways in which people in Goa ar e trying to get round their act against 
this. Instead of jumping from one party to the other, they are resigning from 
their seats. Future historians will refer to chapters like this and this would 
create derision and contempt of our generation who tried to get round the rules 
and tried to invent devices by which yo u can defeat democracy while talking in 
defence of democracy. 
The sixth reason for the decline of democracy is the absence of any 
training course, absence even of any orientation course. Why is it so, Mr. Vice-
Chairman? Leaders arrive at the top. They themselves would never have 
fought an election. Most of them come to Rajya Sabha. Some of them come to 
Rajya Sabha without ever having won an election as an MLA, leave alone the 
Lok Sabha election. And the result is, you find inexperienced people running 
party organisations. And when they are inexperienced, they should have, at 
least, the humility to pick up the robes by undergoing training courses and 
orientation courses. Even in advanced c ountries, there are training courses. 
But we do not have them. The Parliament, of course, conducts such training 
courses; the Secretariats conduct them. But, at the party level, training courses 
are particularly neglected. 
The seventh reason, of course, is the low level of political morality. 
We are willing to change parties, labels, as we change our clothes.   The 
shameful record of defections in our country will go down in the history as 
464 

[9 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
one of the shameful records in any democratic country anywhere in the world.   
I recall the statistics of defections...

During the period between the Fourth and the Fifth General

I have no time to get into the educational system. My point was

I thank you for giving these extra two minutes. I wish to invite the

the Motion of Thanks moved by my distinguished senior colleague, Dr. Karan 
Singh. Sir, I take this opportunity to congratulate the UPA Government under 
the charismatic leadership of Dr. Manmohan Singhji for this  second  Address

the Congress President, Shrimati Soniaji for excellently guiding the UPA as its 
chairperson towards the sole goal of progress and prosperity of the nation, and 
I do hope that the nation will, certainl y, achieve the goals under the UPA 
regime. 
Sir, I welcome the announcement made in the President's Address 
about creation of the Disaster Management Authority through a legislation. The 
country has recently been devastat ed by Tsunami. The entire Andaman and 
Nicobar Islands, many parts of Tam il Nadu, Pondicherry, Kerala and Andhra 
Pradesh have been devastated, killing p eople, making millions of people 
homeless, children orphaned, women widowed and crops washed away. The 
Government and the people together are busy in rehabilitation works. Sir, more 
attention has to be paid to the surviving old persons, widows, orphans and 
physically challenged ones. There are ot her natural disasters like consistent 
drought conditions in my home State of  Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil 
Nadu and in other parts of the country. The farmers are committing suicides 
and fields have parched. I hope this Authority will manage the after-effects of 
national disasters. 
Sir, I appreciate that the Address has ensured communal harmony 
and a new sense of hope to the minorities and weaker sections of the society. 
Now, no more communal riots like the ones in Gujarat w ill be repeated. The 
minorities like Muslims, Christians and others will feel secure under the UPA 
regime. However, the not affected people of Gujarat and also the earthquake 
victims are yet to be rehabilitated. 
Sir, I welcome the announcement made in the President's Address 
that a white paper on the st atus of minorities will be prepared. I demand that it 
should also throw light on the divisive policies and deeds of communal forces 
which are bent upon dividing us on religious and communal lines, and such 
organisations should be banned. 
Sir, I appreciate the concern shown by the Address about Adivasis 
and the promise to grant them rights for cult ivating in forest areas of the forest 
villages. But, they face other problems. They are exploited by forest personnel 
and money-lenders. The tribal girls and women are sexually exploited. The 
tribal girls are lured to cities on the pretext of employment and good life, but 
are forced into flesh trade. This has to be dealt with sternly. The forest officials 
found guilty of exploitation of tribals should be 
466 

[9 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA  
summarily dismissed and arrested for trial. Trafficking in tribal girls should be 
slapped with capital punishment. 
Sir, the introduction of reservation Bill in Parliament is a welcome 
step. It will give requisite mandatory protection to the SC, ST and OBC 
Government employees for their entry, promotional avenues, etc., in 
Government service. But, there is another exploited lot in the society which 
also needs to be given reservation. They are the women of this great country, 
who have to be made economically independent. Hence, I demand that a 
percentage of quota in the Reservation Bill should be reserved for them. 
Sir, the Address promises for en hancing public investment in 
irrigation and wasteland development. These are laudable steps. Irrigation 
facilities need to be developed in a big way. I suggest that wasteland areas be 
allotted to cooperatives of youths and they should be supplied saplings, seeds 
and other things to make wastelands cu ltivable so that the problem of 
unemployment is also tackled. 
Sir, another welcome step in the Pr esident's Address is the promise 
to effect a steep increase in credit fl ow to agriculture. Fo r this, the banking 
sector has to gear up in the true sense. Most of the public sector banks do not 
even fulfil the quota of 18 per cent lending of their net credit to agriculture. The 
private sector banks and more so the foreign banks are too far behind, 
whereas they have to follow the national policies. So, the Government and the 
RBI have to ensure that all the banks implement the Government policies in 
letter and spirit. 
The Address also speaks about the need for mass action for the 
conservation of water. For this, roof top rainwater harvesting has to be made 
compulsory throughout the country. I am  consistently suggesting that the 
Government should create rainwater-harvesting infrastructure in Government 
residential colonies, office complexes, etc.; and for the general public, subsidy 
on such infrastructure needs to be given. Unless we make rainwater 
harvesting compulsory turning it into a mass movement, the scarcity of water 
is not going to be solved. 
Sir, another laudable point in the Addr ess is that the Government will 
actively involve Panchayati-raj Inst itutions in the implementation of 
developmental programmes. We must welcome this but some reforms have to 
be made in the Panchayats also. As per media reports, in Rajasthan, women 
Panch and Sarpanch are elected, but de facto Panch and Sarpanch

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005]

Panchayati-Raj Institutions have to be ensured freedom in their working. I 
hope the Government will take note of this. 
The Address has ensured that Government will give priority to issues 
of both access and excellence in education. I urge upon the Government to 
focus on the education of girls who remain illiterate due to various social and

Sir, I welcome the announcement  that Government proposes to

gynaecologists and lady doctors so that  womenfolk could, at least, tell about

Sir, my last point is about covered latrines in every rural household for 
the women and children. The agony of women and girls who have to attend to 
the call of nature in the open can be imagined. This will require enough money 
but a provision has to be made. I hope, it will be certainly made. 
Sir, I once again support the Motion and thank you very much.

National Policy on voluntary sector 
*122. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH : Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the status of the National Policy on the voluntary sector prepared by 
previous Government; and 
(b) the plans of Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) and (b)AStatement is laid on the Table 
of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) A meeting of leading repr esentatives of the voluntary sector 
was convened on 18th February, 2005 to invite their response on whether or 
not a National Policy on Voluntary Sector is considered desirable and to 
discuss the draft, nature, scope and content of such a Policy. Draft Policy was 
circulated to them in advance. With the exception of only one participant, the 
entire cross-section of participants endorsed the need for a National Policy. In 
the meeting, it was also decided that the Draft Policy on this complex sector 
having lot of diversity requires thorough revision. To revise the Draft, it was 
proposed to constitute Expert Groups having members from voluntary sector 
to work on different sub-heads of the Draft Policy.

*123. SHRIMATI N. P. DURGA:  Will the PRIME MINISTER be

(a)whether it is a fact that Government have identified 137 backward 
districts in the country for development at an estimated cost of Rs. 45 crores; 
(b)if so, the details of the districts that have been identified in the State of 
Andhra Pradesh; 
(c) the criteria adopted in identifying the districts for development; 
 
(d) whether the Government are thinking of developing some of the above 
districts or all the 137 districts as model districts in the country; and 
(e) the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M. V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table 
of the House. 
Statement 
(a) The Government have identified 147 districts, 115 backward districts 
and 32 districts affected by left wing extremism, for funding under the 
Backward Districts Initiative of the Rashtriya Sam Vikas Yojana. A sum of 
Rs. 45 crore is to be provided for each district over a period of three years on 
100 per cent grant basis linked with the satisfactory progress of schemes 
included in the District Plans, 
(b) Ten districts of Andhra Pradesh ar e covered under the programme, 
namely, Adilabad, Warangal, Chittor, Mahbubnagar, Vijayanagaram, 
Karimnagar, Khammam, Medak, Nalgonda and Nizamabad. 
(c) For the non-Special Category States and Assam, the backward districts 
have been identified on the basis of an index of backwardness comprising 
three parameters with equal weights to each, namely, value of output per 
agricultural worker, agricultural wage rate and percentage of SC/ST 
population. For the remaining Special Category States, the identification has 
been made on the recommendation of the State

been identified keeping in view the intensity of left wing extremist violence. 
(d) No, Sir. 
(e) Does not arise.

Statement 
(a) As per the Khadi and Village Industries Commission Act, 1956, the 
functions of the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) are to 
plan, promote, organise and assist in the establishment and development of 
khadi and village industries in the rural areas. Hence the KVIC does not 
directly undertake any production activity. However, through its various 
schemes/programmes, the KVIC support s establishment and operation of 
industries in Khadi and Village Industri es (KVI) sector with the help of its 
implementing agencies like registered khadi and village industries institutions 
and State KVI Boards and by individual entrepreneurs. The sales (annual 
turnover) of the units and employment in the KVI sector during the year

the Hon'ble Supreme Court include the following: 
• Undertaking and completing the survey to identify and enumerate 
working children employed in hazardous industries/occupations/ 
processes within a period of six months. 
• Payment of compensation amounting to  Rs. 20,000/- for every child 
employed in hazardous industri es/occupations/processes by the 
offending employer.  
• Constitution of Child Labour Rehabilitation-cum-Welfare Fund. 
• Investment of the corpus of the fund in a manner, which will yield the 
best possible return. 
• Giving alternative employment to an able bodied adult member of 
every family, which had sent its child (children) for employment in 
hazardous industry/occupation/process. In the event of failure to do so, 
ensure deposit by the State Government @ Rs. 5000/- per child into the 
corpus of the Child Labour Rehabilitation-cum-Welfare Fund. 
• Provision of access to educationa l opportunity to  all children 
withdrawn from hazardous work in a suitable educational institution. 
• Providing access to educational opportunity for at least two hours a day 
for children in non-hazardous jobs and permitting them to work from 
four to six hours a day. 
42 

[10 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
• Opening a separate Cell in the Labour Deptt. of the State Government 
and entrusting the responsibility of monitoring to the Secretary of that 
Deptt. 
• Making Inspectors appointed under Section 17 of the Child Labour 
(Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 fully accountable to the District 
Magistrate and the latter to keep a close and constant surveillance on 
the performance of these Inspectors. 
The Status of the implementation of the directions of the Hon'ble Supreme 
Court is reported in the form of affidavits filed by the Ministry of Labour and 
Employment from time to time. So far, the Ministry has filed affidavits in the 
Hon'ble Court for five times. The last  affidavit was filed on 4th December, 
2003. 
Since 1997-98, till 2002-03, under the Child Labour (Prohibition and 
Regulation) Act, 1986,17.41 lakhs inspections were carried out and 93,493 
violations were detected resulting in 33,000 prosecutions and 14,564 
convictions. 
Child Labour Rehabilitation-cum-Welfare Fund has been set up in all the 
States were child labour exists in hazardous occupations. Since 1997-98, till 
2002-03, an amount of Rs. 1.32 crores has been recovered as compensation 
from the offending employers, Rs. 3.42 crores as contribution of the State 
Governments in the Child Labour Rehabilitation-cum-Welfare Fund and the 
total corpus of the Fund is Rs. 7.34 crores. The Fund is being used by the 
State Governments for the welfare of the working children and their families. 
Special Cell for Child Labour has been set up in all the States and Union 
Territories where child labour exists, except Uttaranchal.

Financial implications and viability of the new regime 
937. DR. AKHILESH DAS: Will th e Minister of COMMUNICATIONS 
AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) announced 
a long awaited Access Deficit Charge ( ADC) regime aimed at reducing long 
distance STD call charges and boosting the rural telephone operations; 
(b) if so, the details of the new regime, indicating the financial 
implications and viability thereof and the major objectives of the new 
regime; and 
(c) the reactions and responses of the private telecom operators to the new 
regime? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. 
SHAKEELAHMAD): (a) to (c) 
63 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2005] 
On 6th January, 2005, the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) 
announced a revised Access Deficit Char ge (ADC) regime effective from 01 
-02-2005. This was part of the annual review as announced by TRAI in its 
last Interconnection Usage Charge (IUC) Regulation effective from 
01.2.2004. The new regime envisages reduction in ADC contribution for 
national long distance calls to 30 paise from earlier slab of 30 p, 50 p and 80 
p and for international long distance calls it envisages reduction in ADC to 
Rs. 2.50 per minute for outgoing calls and Rs. 3.25 for incoming calls as 
against ADC of Rs. 4.25 per minut e applicable for both incoming and 
outgoing calls earlier. As per TRAI, the other salient features, inter-alia 
include: 
(i) Total amount of ADC for Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited (BSNL) kept 
unchanged. 
(ii) Disbursement of ADC altered to ensure that amount of ADC received is 
unchanged while reducing the burden on customers. 
(iii) BSNL only and not the other fixed line operators to receive ADC on all 
incoming international calls and outgoing calls from mobile and 
Wireless Local Loop (Limited Mobility). 
(iv) Key objective emphasis include re ducing the domestic call charges for 
the consumers, addressing grey international calls through a 
combination of policy relating to incentive (arbitrage) margin and 
disincentive (monitoring and penalty) for such calls, ensuring that 
benefit is not passed on to the foreign carriers and consumers at the cost 
of domestic consumers and operators. 
(v) The "other fixed line operators" will retain ADC only on their outgoing 
calls. ADC on all other calls will be provided to BSNL. 
(vi) The details of ADC in rupees per minute applicable for various types of 
calls are enclosed in the Statement (See below). 
(vii) TRAI will examine the implementation of the new rates with latest 
information after three to six months of implementation of the regime, 
without any further consultation process. 
(viii) New consultation process to begin soon on various matters, including 
admissibility of ADC amounts for BSNL, other service providers, for 
WLL (F), likely disbursement of USO amounts, and the 
Interconnection Usage Charge regime. 
64 

[10 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
The long distance tariffs are expected to come down with reduction in 
ADC. Some private operators have anno unced reduction in tariffs for long 
distance calls. According to available information, BSNL, the incumbent has 
not announced any tariff reductions as it has reported that its tariff are already 
generally stated to be even lower than the tariff of private operators. 
The Cellular Operators Association of  India (COAI) has welcomed small 
reduction in ADC burden on the Indian consumers but is of the view that this 
relief is a case of 'too little too late'. It has further stated that reducing ADC 
on incoming international long distance calls does not help Indian consumers 
in any manner. The new regime would not be effective in discouraging grey 
market activities. There is no justification for payment of ADC to Wireless 
Local Loop (WLL) (F) but not to Cellular. 
The Association of Unified Telecom Service Providers of India (AUSPI) 
has stated that the new ADC regime is a major setback to the fixed line 
services because of its inequitable di stribution of ADC only to the largest 
competitor, it had filed a petition in the Telecom Disputes Settlement and 
Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT) against the aforesaid ADC regime. Mahanagar 
Telephone Nigam Limited has also filed a petition in TDSAT against the new 
regime. 
Moreover, TRAI has filed a writ petition in the High Court of Delhi 
against TDSAT and others challenging the jurisdiction of TDSAT for 
adjudicating the matter. 
According to TRAI, the amount of ADC to be provided to BSNL is 
estimated to be around Rs. 2348 crores for a period of six months from 
February to July, 2005. The ADC forecast figures for full year estimated to 
be Rs. 4954 crores for BSNL, which is comparable with previous ADC 
estimation of Rs. 4792 crores. Howeve r, BSNL has stated that it expect 
reduction in amount by Rs. 1254 crores. 
It is difficult to assess the exact impact  as traffic pattern is fast changing 
due to unprecedented subscriber growth. Further, TRAI has stated that this 
regime will be reviewed in a period of three to six months.

961. SHRI DATTA MEGHE: Will the Minister of COMMUNICATIONS 
AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) the total number of Extra Departmental Postal Staff (Gramin Dak 
Sevak) working in rural areas of the country; 
(b) whether these postal employees are given pension after their 
retirement; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor and by when Government propose to 
98 

[10 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
bring crores of workers of the unorganized sector under social security; and 
(e) whether Government have any proposal to give pension to these 
Gramin Dak Sevaks? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. 
SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) 2,98,571 Gramin Dak Sevaks earlier called Extra 
Departmental Agents are working in  rural areas of the country as on 
31.3.2004. 
(b) No, Sir. 
(c) Does no arise in view of (b). 
(d) The Gramin Dak Sevaks hold civil posts under the administrative 
control of the State which is outside the regular civil service and they do not 
come under the unorganized sector. The terms and conditions of employment 
of Gramin Dak Sevaks are governed by the Department of Posts Gramin Dak 
Sevaks (Conduct and Employment) Rules, 2001. Gramin Dak Sevaks are not 
entitled for pension after retirement. 
On the pattern of Fifth Central Pay Commission set up for regular 
Government employees, a one-man Comm ittee headed by Justice Charnjit 
Talwar, retired Judge of Delhi High Court was set up by the department on 
31.3.1995 to examine the wage structure and service conditions of Extra 
Departmental Agents. The Committee submitted its report to the Government 
on 30.4.97. The Government examined the report of the said Committee and 
issued a package of benefits, in full and final settlement of the Justice Talwar 
Committee recommendations. 
The following terminal benefits are admissible to Gramin Dak Sevaks 
Severance Amount of Rs.20,000/- to Rs. 30,000/- depending upon 
length of employment. 
Ex-gratia gratuity of Rs.18,000/-depending upon length of 
employment after minimum 10 years of employment. 
Group Insurance of Rs. 10,000/- under Extra Departmental Agents 
Group Insurance Scheme 1992. 
(e) In view of the above, there is no proposal for grant of pension to the 
Gramin Dak Sevaks.

113 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2005] 
deployed on the ground in Sri Lanka. This included about 700 US Marines. 
This excludes US personnel manning ships deployed off the coast of Sri 
Lanka who would probably have numbered between 700 to 900. 
The Tsunami disaster in Sri Lanka and other Indian Ocean rim countries 
attracted a very high degree of international attention and evoked an 
enormous outpouring of compassion and international assistance to the 
affected countries, includ ing Sri Lanka. The scale of the devastation caused 
was so great that all relief contributions were welcome. India was a key 
player in this major international humanitarian effort in Sri Lanka and other 
affected countries and was, alongwith  the United States, a member of the 
Core Group that coordinated relief in the initial phases. 
The India Navy launched "Operation Rainbow" the day the Tsunami 
struck. The first Indian naval Dornier carrying 650kg of medical supplies and 
a medical team arrived in Sri La nka on December 26 itself. Almost 
simultaneoulsy, four Indian naval ships steamed towards the ports of Galle 
and Trincomalee. These vessels, which picked up relief supplies on the way, 
reached Sri Lanka just over 24 hours afterwards and immediately commenced 
relief and damage control operations. This deployment was stepped up to 
include stationing of an air detachment of ten aircraft for three weeks, about 
fifteen naval ship-loads of supplies, fifteen medical teams includings a 
mobile field hospital (140 men) that was airlifted and specialist doctors, a 45-
bed hospital ship (INS Jamuna) that wa s anchored of Galle and Trincomalee 
for two weeks, ten teams of naval divers and a 81 -member composite Army 
disaster management team. 
Sri Lankan President Kumaratunga, Pr ime Minister Rajapakse and several 
Sri Lankan Ministers have expressed the gratitude of the people of Sri Lanka 
for Indian assistance. President Ku maratunga also dispatched Foreign 
Minister Lakshman Kadirgamar as Special Envoy to thank India for its 
generous contribution to the relief efforts.

Stabilisation of Nuclear Interface between India and Pakistan 
988 SHRI VI JAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that in the emerging global security 
environment, conventional military conflicts between Nation States may 
assume nuclear overtones, resulting in devastation on unprecedented scale; 
and 
(b) if so, what steps, at diplomatic level or through people-to-people 
contact, are envisaged between India and Pakistan to stabilise their nuclear 
interface so that such a catastrophe c ould be avoided for all time to come, 
even if minor irritants continue to be discussed and gradually solved through 
on-going official and non-official delegations meeting each other, 
periodically? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI RAO INDERJIT SINGH): (a) India has consistently 
maintained that the threat to international peace and security posed by the use 
or threat of use of nuclear weapons ca nnot be eliminated as long as such 
weapons are not eradicated comple tely through universal and non-
discriminatory instruments. India has taken a number of initiatives in the UN 
General Assembly in this regard including tabling of annual resolutions 
"Convention on the Prohibition of the Use of Nuclear Weapons" and 
"Reducing Nuclear Danger", which have been adopted by a majority. 
However, regrettably there has been no progress towards this goal. 
(b) As a part of the process of composite dialogue between India and 
Pakistan, which commenced in February, 2004, two rounds of expert level 
dialogue on Nuclear Confidence Building Measures have been held on 19-20 
June, 2004 (New Delhi) and 14-15 December, 2004 (Islamabad). At the June, 
2004 meeting, both sides had inter-alia agreed, in principle, to conclude an 
Agreement on pre-notification of flight tests of ballistic missiles, a draft to 
which was handed over to Pakistan. Substantive discussions on the proposed 
Agreement were held during December, 2004 and further discussions are due 
to take place. The two sides have also held discussions on early 
operationalisation of the decision taken to upgrade the existing hotline 
between the DGMOs, and to establish a dedicated and secure hotline between 
two Foreign Secretaries. These measures are inter-alia intended to prevent 
misunderstanding and reduce risks relevant to nuclear issues.

1027. SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the percentage of population below poverty line according to the latest 
available report, State-wise; 
(b) the change in the percentage of BPL families during the last five years;

families; 
(d) the income limit to identify the BPL families; and 
(e) the base-year of this income-limit and the necessity of changing it in 
the context of present day scenario? 
150 

[10 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) The Planning Commission estimates 
poverty at national and State level from the large sample surveys on 
household consumer expenditure conducted by the National Sample Survey 
Organization (NSSO) at an interval of approximately five years. The latest 
such survey was conducted in 1999-2000 (NSS 55 th Round). The State-wise 
table on percentage of population living below poverty line in the country for 
both rural and urban areas in 1999-2000 is given th Statement (see below). 
(b) Planning Commission estimates the percentage of BPL population and 
not the BPL families. Based on the data of the latest two surveys of NSSO 
for the period 1993-94 (50 th round) and 1999-2000 (55 th Round), the 
percentage of population living in the country has been estimated as 36% in 
1993-94 and 26.1% in 1999-2000 below poverty line. 
(c) Yes, Sir. There are several programmes being implemented by 
Ministry of Rural Development for upliftment of BPL families. These are (i) 
Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yoja na; (ii)Sampoorna Grameen Rozgar 
Yojana; (iii) Indira Awaas Yojana; and (iv) National Food for Work 
Programme. 
(d) The Planning Commission has adopted per capita consumption 
expenditure as the criterion to determine the persons living below the poverty 
line and not income limit precisely for two reasons. First expenditure data 
reflect more accurately people's actual level of living while income data are 
more concerned with people's potential level of living. Secondly, expenditure 
data are considered more reliable th an income data. The persons with 
monthly per capita expenditure below the prescribed limit of Rs. 327.56 in 
rural areas and Rs. 454.11 in urban areas are considered to be living below 
the poverty line in 1999-2000. 
(e) The monthly per capita expenditure of Rs. 49.09 in rural areas and Rs. 
56.64 in urban areas is the expenditure limit prescribed for identifying the 
BPL population at national level for the base year 1973-74. These 
expenditure limits for 1973-74 are updated for price-rise in subsequent years, 
that is, the years in which the quinquennial rounds are conducted by NSSO 
(1977-78,1983,1987-88,1993-94 and 1999-2000).

Resource invested in manpower 
1030. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that lack of trained staff 
coupled with inadequate computing machines has resulted in the country 
being ten years behind in weather prediction as compared to the West; 
(b) whether it is a fact that in developed countries about 70 per cent of the 
resources are invested on manpower, while in India it is mere 20 per cent; 
and 
(c) if so, the steps Government proposes to take to invest in trained 
manpower and computers to analyse the available information for better 
weather predictions? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPILSIBAL): (a) Yes, Sir. Not enough investment 
has been made in the recent past for acquiring state-of-the-art technology for 
weather prediction. The equipment needs to be upgraded and number of earth 
observatories are to be increased alongwith the installation of automatic rain 
gauges and other equipment to enable  IMD to predict more accurately the 
prevalent weather conditions. The Department is 125 years old with a lot of 
dedicated scientific manpower. IMD ha s a well organized training institute 
imparting training to its officers and staff and also to the officers from Indian 
Navy, Coast-Guard, Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology etc. and 
developing countries of south-east Asia and Africa. IMD's Central Training 
Institute at Pune is functioning as one of the Regional Meteorological 
Training Centers of the World Meteorological Organisation, Geneva. 
As a lot of other Departments also seek to reply on weather predictions for 
their work such as Tourism and Civil Aviation, Agriculture, etc. the 
requirements in terms of accuracy/periodicity have gone up. IMD needs to 
restructure to meet the emerging needs of the nation. 
(b) Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) do not have data on 
155 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2005] 
percentage investment by the Government on trained labour vis-a-vis the 
figures in developed countries. The ba sic issue is collection, analysis and 
dissemination of information. For this world would class technology and 
human resources are required. This is essential for meeting the emerging 
needs of the Indian economy and other Government Departments. 
(c) Yes, Sir. IMD has prepared a proposal to upgrade its existing 
forecasting services. The project details are being finalized. The project shall 
be implemented in a phased manner during the present and next five year 
plan period.

(b) The India Meteorological Department (IMD) follows a four stage 
warning system for issuing warning for tropical cyclones. A "Pre-cyclone 
Watch" is issued whenever a depression forms over the Bay of Bengal or 
Arabian Sea. This is followed by a "Cyclone Alert" issued 2-3 days in 
advance of commencement of bad wheat her along the coast. In the third 
stage, Cyclone Warnings are issued 1- 2 days in advance which specify the 
expected place and time of landfall of th e tropical cyclone. The final stage is 
known as "post-landfall Outlook" which is issued 12 hours in advance of 
landfall and contains location specific forecast of landfall alongwith other 
warning details. 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) The accuracy of cyclone forecasts issued by IMD is generally on 
156 

[10 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
par with the accuracy of such forecasts issued by the tropical cyclone forecast 
services of other developed countries like USA, Japan, Australia etc. 
However, with the development of new observing systems such as buoys, 
Doppler Radars and new generation satellites, these forecasts are likely to 
improve further. Four Doppler Weather Radars (DWRs) have started 
functioning along the east coast of Kolkata, Machilipatnam, Chennai and 
Sriharikota. The existing Cyclone warning radar atVisakhapatnam will be 
replaced by DWR by the middle of this year. DWR has the capability of 
providing accurate wind structure of Tropical Cyclone. 
A dedicated Indian geostationary meteorological satellite (now named 
Kalpana-I) was launched in September, 2002 and is providing high 
resolution cloud imageries in the Visibl e, Infrared (IR) and Water Vapour 
channels. Similarly the INSAT-3Awhich was launched in April 2003, 
provides statellite imageries of 1 km. resolution. INSAT-3D is likely to be 
launched in 2006, which will have improved capabilities.

HIGHWAYS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) The proposed Sethu Samudram Ship

aimed at informing the general public as well as the environmentalists that a

viability of the project, further, the alignment has been chosen 
176 

[10 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA

with mathematical modeling carried our by the NEERI indicates that the 
apprehensions of damage to the coral r eefs and flora and fauna in the project

significant impact on the fishing activities in the region. A detailed 
Environmental Management Plan has been drawn up for inter alia ensuring 
that the marine environment is monitored continuously during the execution 
of the project.

commencement of the work after obtaining the mandatory approvals.

I deem it a great privilege to stand here before this august House to express 
to respected Rashtrapatiji a profound sens e of gratitude for his Address to the 
two Houses of our Parliament. I deem it a privilege for more than one reason

gratitude to the President. Last year, in  his Address, the President highlighted 
the provisions underlying the Common Minimum Programme. This year's 
Budget complements and supplements t hat Address because it outlines a 
programme of action to realise the goals and objectives we have outlined in 
our Common Minimum Programme. 
At the very outset, I would like to touc h upon the issue of gender inequality 
and the hardships that out women have to undergo, to which the hon. Member 
Shrimati Sarla Maheshwariji had drawn our attention. I stand committed to 
doing all that is possible to end gender discrimination in all its forms. With 
regard to the reservation issue, our Gove rnment is seized of the matter; the 
hon. Home Minister is already engaging in a dialogue with all political parties. 
It will be our effort to bring this legislation for enactment before both the 
Houses as early as possible. Sir, all the Members, who have spoken in this 
debate, have made very valuable suggestions. It is not possible for me to 
touch upon all these suggestions. But I assure the hon. Members that I have 
taken note of their concerns, and in days and months to come, we will reflect 
on all those concerns in our Policy Planning fora. 
The hon. Leader of the Opposition, my esteemed friend and colleague,

fully prepared to match up to the best available knowledge base anywhere in 
the world. Education once again is of top priority. When I look at what is 
happening in countries like South Korea, I find all secondary school age 
children are in schools. But we are now here there. Enrolement rates in our 
country in primary schools and elementary schools have gone up but the drop

In particular, in our school system the teaching of Science and Mathematics 
requires a fresh

look, in several parts of our country, the teaching of Mathematics and Science

as it ought to be, if India has to generate enough number of scientists and 
technologists. I sincerely hope that  this Knowledge Commission will address 
all these issues and come forward with a blueprint for purposeful action to

I shall now deal with some of the issues which have been mentioned by the

STATEMENTS BY MINISTER 
Constitution of National Disaster Management Authority 
THE MINISTER OF HOME (SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL): Sir, the country has 
witnessed some major disasters in the past few years; with the super cyclone 
in Orissa in the year 1999, the earthquake in Bhuj in 2001 and the recent 
Tsunami. In the light of these exper iences, a need has been felt for an 
institutional mechanism which would facilitate drawing up and implemenation 
of plans and projects for mitigation of disasters; taking appropriate preparatory 
measures by various authorities/departm ents; and for coordinating response 
and relief after a disaster strikes. 
The approach to disaster management has so far been reactive— 
responding to disasters after they occur.  Not much attention has been paid to 
mitigation, it is possible to ensure this, provided appropriate mitigation 
measures are taken so that the next calamity does not result in the loss of 
property and lives as hitherto fore. It  will be the endeavour of the Government 
to ensure that over a period of time this objective is achieved. 
Whereas it has been widely accepted t hat the country's response to the 
recent Tsunami was prompt and effective, it  is felt that the response to future 
disasters can be better if appropriate preparedness and capacity measures 
are put in place. A need has also been fe lt over time to vest the coordination 
mechanism with the necessary legislative back up to enable holistic 
coordination of resources for response. 
In the light of the abov e requirements, it is proposed to enact a law on 
disaster management which will provide for the requisite institutional and 
coordination mechanism and powers for undertaking the mitigation measures 
as also mechanism for ensuring preparedness and capacity building to handle 
disasters. The Disaster Management Bill,  2005 is proposed to be introduced 
in the current Budget Session of the Parliament. 
312 

[10 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
In the light of the above requirements and keeping in view that the passage 
of the Bill is likely to take some time, it is proposed to provide for the requisite 
institutional and coordination mechanism and powers for undertaking 
mitigation measures as also mechanism for ensuring preparedness and 
capacity building to handle disasters duri ng the interim period. It is, therefore, 
proposed to set up a National Disaster Management Authority as associated 
Committees by executive orders immediately, in accordance with the 
provisions of the pro posed Bill, pending enactment of the law. These 
institutional and coordination mechanisms will be modified in the line with 
statutory provisions after the passage of the Bill. 
In the meantime, action has already been taken to earmark 8 battalions of 
Central Para Military Forces, from thei r existing strength, to be trained and 
equipped to function as specialist response teams. Training of trainers for 
responding to natural disasters has been completed. Similar training for 
responding to radiological, biological and chemical emergencies has also 
been undertaken. 18 specialist response teams have already been trained for 
responding to natural disaster. 
Communication is of the utmost impor tance in coordinating response to a 
disaster. An Emergency Communication Plan has been approved and is 
under implementation for providing comm unication linkages among national, 
State and District level Emergency Operation Centres and the Mobile 
Communication Units to be set up at the sites of disasters. 
The National Institute of Disaster Management was set up through issue of 
an executive order is October, 2003. A fter the passage of the Bill, necessary 
notification for setting up of the Nation al Institute of Disaster Management will 
be issued with appropriate modifications, if  any, to ensure that it conforms 
with the law.

75TH ANNIVERSARY OF DANDI MARCH 
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: As the hon. Members are aware, on the 12th 
March, 2005, the nation celebrates the 75th Anniversary of the Dandi March. On 
this historic occasion, the Father of the Nation, Mahatma Gandhi, along with 
several patriotic volunteers, challenged the imposition of Salt Tax by the British 
Government. The non-violent protest through the medium of Salt Satyagraha 
had an appeal across regional, class and ethnic boundaries throughout the 
country.

and the non-violent Satyagrahis whose heroic efforts contributed towards the 
independence of the country.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Banned medicines 
*141. SHRI SHAHID SIDDIQUI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that many medicines, used in 
India, are banned abroad for a long time; 
(b) if so, the details of those medicines alongwith their names; and 
(c) whether Government have taken any action to ban them in India; if so, the 
details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMDOSS): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 

RAJYA SABHA [11 March, 2005] 
Statement 
There is no system of global banning of drugs. Certain drugs and 
formulations withdrawn in one or more countries may continue to be 
marketed in other countries. The decision to ban a drug by the regulatory 
authorities is normally based on the risk assessment process which is 
influenced by a number of factors such as disease pattern in a country, 
indications and dosages of the drug permitted, varying reactions of certain ethnic 
groups in a given population, availability of safer substitutes and overall safety 
profile of the drug. It is a well-known fact that administration of any drug is not 
absolutely free from side effects or adverse reactions in a statistically 
insignificant minority of the population. 
There is an adequate mechanism in India to review the status of the drug 
formulation as and when any serious adverse event is reported in the 
International journals, WHO Newsletters or when a drug formulation is 
reported to have been withdrawn in some countries. The use of the drug, so 
reported, is assessed in consultation with the experts, based on available 
technical information, benefit-risk ratio, local needs etc. The matter is further 
considered by the Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB), a statutory body 
under the Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940. 
Seventy six categories of drug formulations have so far been prohibited in the 
country by the Central Government, which were considered irrational or 
harmful in the context of present knowledge. In the recent past, drugs like 
Astemizole, Terfinadine and Rofecoxib have been prohibited after due 
assessment of their benefit-risk ratio by the experts, while drugs like Analgin, 
Hydroxyquinoline, Furazolidone, Phenylpropanolamine, Nimesulide etc. have 
been permitted to be continued to be marketed after due examination of their 
safety and use in the country. 
A National Pharmacovigilance Programme has been launched in 2004 to 
capture data on adverse reactions to drug use in the country.

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMDOSS): (a) and (b) Astatement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
Cholera, viral hepatitis, enteric fever and acute diarrhoeal diseases are the main 
water borne diseases caused by contamination of water with virus, bacteria 
parasites. The number of patients suffering from these water, borne diseases during 
the period from 2002 to 2004, State/Union Territory-wise and disease-wise is 
annexed as Statement-I (See below). The relevant data on the rural-urban basis is 
not centrally maintained. 
Health is primarily a State subject and provision of medical relief for water 
borne diseases like cholera etc. through primary and community health centres 
is looked after by the State Government. Unsafe drinking water, poor sanitation 
and hygiene are some of the causes of water borne diseases. The preventive 
measures taken by the local health authorities include privision of safe 
drinking water, improvement of personnel and community hygiene, safe 
disposal of human excreta, undertak ing appropriate health education, 
surveillance and monitoring, distribution of chlorine tablets and ORS packets 
etc. 
The Government of India supplements the efforts of the State 
Government/Union Territories by providing funds under the Accelerated Rural 
Water Supply Programme,  Accelerated Urban Water Supply Programme, 
Total Sanitation Campaign,School Sanitation and Hygiene Education and Low 
Cost Sanitation Scheme for tackling quality related problems is respect of 
rural and urban drinking water supply. National Institute of Communicable 
Diseases, Delhi (NICD) provides techni cal support to the State Governments 
and undertake surveillance, early detection and prevention and control of 
outbreaks of communicable diseases including water borne diseases. Technical 
support to improve the quality of drinking water is also envisaged to be 
provided by NICD, Delhi. 
The Government of India has launched an Integrated Disease Surveillance 
Programme in November, 2004, to further strengthen identification of 
outbreaks of various diseases including water-borne diseases like Typhoid, 
Cholera, Jaundice etc. So that ear ly intervention could be made and 
occurrence, disability and death due to various diseases could be reduced.

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI

Statement 
(a) The funds for implementation of National AIDS Control Programme 
Phase II are provided in lump sum to all the AIDS Control Societies and anti-
AIDS drugs are part of this. Statement-I indicating release of funds to all the 
State AIDS Control Societies (SACS) during the last three years is annexed.

(b) Yes, Sir. Anti-AIDS drugs are provided free of charge through 25 ART 
Centres established in selected Government medical institutions in 13 States of 
the country. The Anti Retroviral drugs used for treatment of AIDS patients 
through these ART Centers are the triple drug combination generic drugs 
manafactured by pharmaceutical companies based in India. The triple drug 
combination for AIDS patients not having TB include 
21
