Stavudine, it is replaced by Zidovudine. For AIDS patients with tuberculosis 
co-infection drug Nevirapine is replaced by Efavirenz. These drugs improve 
quality of life and longevity of AIDS patients but do not cure HIV/AIDS 
completely. 
(c) National AIDS Control Programme for prevention and control of HIV/ 
AIDS is a comprehensive programme .-and is being implemented in the country 
through 35 State AIDS Control Societies and 3 AIDS Control Societies run by 
the municipal corporations in cities like Mumbai, Chennai and Ahmedabad. The 
programme is  focused on: (i) Intensive IEC (Information, Education and 
Communication) for general population with behaviour change communication 
for high risk groups; (ii) voluntary counseling and testing facilities; (iii) 
provision of safe blood; (iv) control of Sexually transmitted infections through 
STI Clinics and an aggressive condom promotion campaign; (v) establishing 
centres for Prevention of Parents to Child Transmission (PPTCT) and (vi) 
Providing care and support services to people living with HIV/AIDS, 
treatment facilities for Opportunistic Infections in all the Government medical 
colleges and district hospitals, community care centers, Drop-in-Centers and 
provision of free Anti Retroviral drugs through selected Government hospitals.

*154. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA:

(a) whether Government are aware that pr ices of medicines are constantly

within common man's reach; 
(c) whether the Drug Price Control Order, 1995 has left some of the 
essential medicines out of its ambit; 
(d) if so, whether DPCO is proposed to be suitably amended; 
(e) if so, the details thereof; and 
(f) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM 
VILAS PASWAN): (a) to (f) In the last four years the percentage change in 
the wholesale price index (WPI) for drugs and medicines has been 
40 

[11 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
less as compared to all other commodities. During the year 2003-2004 the 
percentage change in the wholesale price index for drugs and medicines was 
2.55 as compared to that for all commodities which was 5.46%. 
The Drug Policies, as amended from time to time, are directed towards 
ensuring abundant availability of quality drugs at reasonable prices. 
Presently 74 bulk drugs specified in th e First Schedule of the Drugs (Prices 
Control) Order, 1995 (DPCO, 95) and the formulations based thereon are 
under price control and their prices are fixed/revised by the National 
Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) in accordance with the provisions 
of the DPCO, 95. These drugs have been identified for inclusion under price 
control in the DPCO, 95 on the basis of criteria mentioned in the 
'Modifications in Drug Policy, 1986', announced in September, 1994. These 
criteria take into account the extent of usage and the market competition in 
various drugs. 
Prices of non-Scheduled formulations are fixed by the manufacturers 
themselves keeping in view the various factors like cost of production, 
marketing/selling expenses, R&D expenses, trade commission, market 
competition, product innovation, product quality etc. The Government takes 
corrective measures where the public interest is found to be adversely 
affected. 
A Committee under the Chairmanship of Joint Secretary (PI) was 
constituted to examine the span of price control (including trade margin) in 
the light of National Common Minimum Programme and the observations of 
the Supreme Court in SLP No. 3668/ 2003 and to suggest measures for 
fulfilling the objective of National Common Minimum Programme to ensure 
the availability of life saving drugs at .reasonable prices. This Committee has 
submitted its interim report to the Government. The Committee has 
recommended, inter-alia, intensive monitoring on the prices of all those 
drugs out of the selected basket (National List of Essential Medicines, 2003) 
which are not under price control, ceiling on trade margins of drugs, a system 
of price negotiations for the new patented drugs, special schemes for people 
below poverty line, introduction of Rajasthan Model of Life Line Fluid 
Stores (hospital pharmacy stores ru n by Medicare Societies) for bulk 
purchase of drugs directly from manufacturer and selling them at reduced 
prices, compounding of offences und er the Essential Commodities Act, 
establishment of DPCO cells in all St ates on the model of Karnataka etc., 
efforts to increase 
41 

RAJYA SABHA [11 March, 2005] 
public awareness, wide publicity to policies and decisions of the Government 
and NPPA etc. 
A Task Force has also been constituted under the Chairmanship of the 
Principal Adviser (PP), Planning Commission to explore various options 
other than price control for achieving the objective of making available life 
saving drugs at reasonable prices. 
In the light of the above, DPCO will be amended, if necessary.

that the MSP covers A2+FL costs (actual expenses paid in cash and kind, 
including rent for leased-in land and imputed value of wages of family 
labour) in high cost States, while it cove rs the C2 cost in low cost States. As 
regards J-34 variety, which is grown in Punjab and Rajasthan, the C2 cost of 
production projected by CACP for 2004-05 in Rajasthan in Rs. 1455.25 per 
quintal while the projected  C2 cost for the same year for Punjab is Rs. 
2316.31 per quintal. The MSP fixed for J-34 variety of cotton in Rajasthan 
for 2004-05 is Rs. 1760 per quintal, whereas, MSP fixed for J-34 in Punjab is 
Rs. 1815 per quintal. Thus, while the MSP covers the projects C2 cost of 
production in Rajasthan, it is below the projected C2 cost production in 
Punjab. However, MSP fixed for J-34 variety of cottion in Punjab covers the 
A2+FL cost projected by CACP at Rs. 1773.37 per quintal in Punjab for 
2004-05. 
(c) and (d) In order to avoid distress sale by farmers, the designated 
agency, namely the Cotton Corporation of India (CCI) procures Kapas (seed 
cotton) at MSP. As on 8th March 2005 the CCI procured 128.80 lakh 
quintals, equivalent to 25.05 lakh lint bales from different cotton growing 
States. In order to strengthen the infrastructure for cottion procurement, the 
Government of India has recently d eclared the National Agricultural Co-
operative Marketing Federation of India Limited (NAFED) as an agency

for undertaking price support operations in cotton, in addition to Cotton

Joint Committee on crop Insurance Scheme 
1091. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKAR AN: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state; 
62 

[11 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) whether it is a fact that a Joint Committee has been constituted to 
review the crop insurance scheme; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the Commitee has submitted its report; and 
(d) if so, the major recommendations of the Committee? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) to (d) A Joint Group was constituted by 
the Government under the Chairmanship of an Add itional Secretary in the 
Ministry of Agriculture with the following terms of reference:— 
(i) To review the status position of existing Crop Insurance Schemes i.e. 
National Agricultural Insurance Scheme  (NAIS), Pilot Project on Farm 
Income Insurance Scheme (FIIS), Varsha Bima Yojana and other agriculture 
related schemes floated by Private General Insurance Companies. 
(ii) Improvements requird in National Agricultural Insurance Scheme. 
(iii) To develop broad parameters/concept paper of an appropriate and 
farmers friendly crop insurance sche me after taking into account of 
professional inputs obtained from experts and private sector general 
insurance companies. 
(iv) To make assessment of up front subsidy, if any, to be paid by the 
government. 
The Group has submitted its report on 20.12.2004. The major 
recommendations of the Group relating to the Crop Insurance are:- 
* Reduction in the unit area of insurance to the level of village 
Panchayat for major crops. 
* Threshold/guaranteed yield is proposed to the based on best 5 years 
out of preceding 7 years yield data. 
* Indemnity levels will be 90% for low risk areas/crops and 80% for 
other areas/crops. 
* Coverage of pre-sowing/planning risks (i.e. prevented sowing on 
account of adverse seasonal cond itions). The indemnity payable 
may range between 20% - 25% of sum insured. 
* Post-harvest losses on account of cyclone are to be covered in 
coastal areas for a period of two weeks from harvesting provided the 
harvested crop is lying in the field. 
63 

RAJYA SABHA [11 March, 2005] 
* Uniform seasonality discipline for loanee and non-loanee farmers is 
to be followed in consultation with the States/UTs. 
* On account payment of claims is to be made during the season on 
the basis of weather data or satellite imagery of other proxy 
indicators so as to make timely payment of claims. 
* An individual assessment of claims will be carried out in case of 
specified localized calamities viz. hailstorm, landslide and damage 
due to wild animals. 
* Insurance scheme to be placed on actuarial regime. However, the 
premium to be paid by the farmers be suitably subsidized. 
* AIC should expand its network in terms of district level franchise, 
rural agents, micro-insurance agents to provide better service to 
farmers, particularly non-loanee farmers.

Policy changes for market access to farmers 
1095. SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JO SHI: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have decided to make major 
policy changes that would remove all restrictions and impediments in the way 
of the farmers having access to markets where they opt in the best prices; and 
(b) if so, the nature of concrete decisions taken, so far and by when these 
are due to be implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) Yes, Sir. The State law dealing with 
agricultural marketing (APMC Act) is a major impediment in providing a free 
marketing environment in the country. The State Governments have been 
advised to amend the APMC Act in order to allow development of 
competitive markets in the private and cooperative sectors to encourage direct 
marketing and contract farming prog rammes and to establish effective 
linkages between farm production and retail chains. 
(b) The Ministry has taken the following steps for implementation of the 
proposed reforms:— 
i) The Ministry organized Na tional Conferences with State 
Governments at New Delhi on 07.01.2004 and at Bangalore on 
19.11.2004 and evolved a consensus on the need for reforms in the 
APMC Act. 
ii) The Ministry circulated a model la w to the States in order to guide 
them in amending the APMC Act.

Scheme on 20.10.2004 for Developoment/Strengthening of 
Marketing Infrastructure, Grading and Standardization. Under this

infrastructure projects will be provided in those States/UTs that 
amend the APMC Act on the lines suggested in the model law.

VILAS PASWAN): (a) and (b) Through the Patents (Amendment) Ordinance

1112. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that drugs containing Phenyl Propanol Amine 
(PPA) for nasal decongestion and considered prone to stroke are banned in 
many parts of world but are freely sold in the country; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps being taken to minimize effect of such formulations in anti-
cold pills to prevent stroke? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) The 
PPA (Phenylpropanolamine) has been used in cough and cold preparations in 
many countries. The PPA containing products were withdrawn in USA in 
November 2000, where these were marketed in higher strengths for weight 
loss in addition to their use in cough and cold preparations. These were 
withdrawn because of a reported risk of Hemorrhagic Stroke indicated by a 
study conducted in Yale University. The Committee on Safety of Medicines 
in UK also examined the safety of PPA  and concluded that the evidence of 
link between Hemorrhagic Stroke and PPA was weak and the formulations 
for cough and cold in low doses could continue to be sold in UK. 
The matter was also simultaneously ex amined in India in 2000-2001 in 
consultation with the experts and it was felt that in view of the similarity of 
use of PPA formulations in India to that of UK, the drug should be permitted 
to be marketed in cough and cold preparation with daily dose not more than 
50mg for children and 10Omg for adults.

HEPATITIS-B & POLIO: 
In order to eradicate Polio, Governme nt has taken effective measures by

Under the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP), vaccines are given 
to the children for protection against 6 preventable diseases of measles, 
diphtheria, pertussis, tuberculosis, tetanus and polio. UIP is implemented by 
the States. 
TUBERCULOSIS: 
To control TB, National Tuberculosis Control Programme (NTCP) was 
launched in the country in 1962. NTCP could not achieve the desired results. 
Therefore, Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP), widely 
known as DOTS which is a WHO recommended strategy is being 
implemented since 1997 in a phased manner with the objective of achieving 
cure rate of 85% of new sputum positive cases and to detect at least 70% of 
such cases, diagnosis by sputum microscopy instead of X-ray helps in 
detecting infectious cases and monitoring their treatment on priority. 
Facilities for diagnosis by sputum micr oscopy have been decentralized and 
strengthened. Drugs are provided free of cost in patient-wise boxes and 
consumed by the patients under direct observation of the DOT provider and 
patients are regularly monitored so that they complete their treatment. 
Presently, more than 950 million population in 547 districts/reporting units 
have been covered under the revised strategy. The Project districts have 
reported cure rate of more than 85% which means that more than 8 out of 
every 10 patients put on treatment under the revised strategy are being 
successfully cured as against below 4 in the earlier programme. To make the 
programme more accessible to larger se gments of the population, and to 
supplement the Government efforts in this direction, emphasis is being given 
to involve the community, medical colleges, all general hospitals, private 
practitioners and NGOs in the programme. 
MALARIA, DENGUE AND KALA-AZAR: 
The Govemment of India implementing comprehensive National Vector 
Borne Diseases Control Programme (N VBDCP) in the entire country for 
prevention and control of vector borne diseases namely Malaria, Filaria, Kala-
azar, Japanese Encephalitis and Dengue . The Government of India provide 
technical support, drugs for treatment of Malaria, Kala-azar and Dengue. 
Insecticides and Larvicides are also provided to the States as per the approved 
pattern. Assistance is provided for training programme and IEC. State 
Governments are responsible for planning, implementation and monitoring of 
the programme. 
Overall incidence of malaria in the country has declined from 2.08 million

Health Policy also envisaged eliminati on of Kaia-azar by the year 2010. The 
following strategies are being adopted to prevent and control Malaria, Kala-

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b)

Government of India has launched a comprehensive National AIDS Control 
Programme, which has the following components:— 
• Preventive interventions for high risk populations through targeted 
interventions adopting a multi-pronged strategy including peer 
counseling and behaviour change communication. 
• Preventive interventions for the general population through 
Information Education and Communication (IEC) programmes for 
blood safety, voluntary counselling and testing services, Prevention 
of Parent to Child Transmission (PPTCT). 
• Provision of low cost care and support services by providing 
community care services, treatment of opportunistic infections and 
prevention of occupational exposure. 
• Collaborative efforts to promote inter-sectoral programme activities 
including work place interventions and public-private partnerships. 
• Build technical and managerial capacities for programme 
implementation through surveillance, training, monitoring and 
evaluation, technical resource gr oups, operational research and 
programme management.

Sexually Transmitted Disease (STD) clinic in each district of the

Health Improvement Programme 
1176.   DR. KARAN SINGH: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the recent study on social progress and outlook made by World 
Bank shows that health indicators in India have not exactly improved and 
shows a mixed bag of results; 
(b) if so, whether according to the study various reasons have been 
mentioned in its survey report; 
(c) whether Government have considered this study report of the World 
Bank regarding the health progress; and 
(d) if so, what are the main  steps that are being considered to improve the 
health programmes as suggested by the survey report? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) 
According to recent study on social progress and outlook made by the World 
Bank, there has been a progressive improvement in certain health indicators, 
viz, life expectancy at birth, Infant Mo rtality Rate (IMR) and malnourished 
children, over last two decades. Howeve r, there is a deterioration in health 
indicators like Maternal Mortality Rate (MMR) and prevalence of HIV. 
(c) and (d) The Report of the World Bank has been considered. The report 
itself has qualified that there are probl ems with the data for the indicator 
(MMR) in some of the largest States that raised questions regarding data at 
the national level. The report of the National Family Health Survey-ll also 
acknowledges that the di fference in the estimate s of MMR of NFHS-I and 
NFHS-II is not statistically significant due to various reasons such as larger 
sampling errors etc. The Sample Regist ration System (SRS) of the Registrar 
General of India have estimated the MMR for the country as 407 per 1,00,000 
live births in 1998 which is the same  period when NFHS-II have estimated 
the MMR as 540 per 1,00,000 live births. It is thus not correct to say that the 
material mortality rate has worsened. 
It is true that the estimated number of HIV infections in the country has 
risen from 3.5 million infections in 1998 to 5.1 million infections in 2003. 
Reasons for rise in HIV positive person s are low awareness of people about 
HIV/AIDS in the country especially rural and female partners in the highly 
vulnerable States; high proportion of migrant population; inadequate 
145 

RAJYA SABHA [11 March, 2005] 
safe sex practices; and large number of vulnerable population. 
In order to accelerate decline of Maternal Mortality Rate, provision has 
been made for upgrading Primary Health Centres for providing 24-hour 
delivery services, operationalising the First Referral units for providing 
Emergency Obsteric Care and training the health staff for providing Skilled 
J3irth Attendance at delivery, under the Second phase of Reproductive and 
Child Health Programme. 
In order to prevent and control th e spread of HIV/AIDS in India, 
Government has launched a comprehensive National AIDS Control 
Programme, currently under implementation throughout the country as a 
centrally sponsored scheme with following components:— 
• Preventive interventions for high-risk populations through targeted 
interventions adopting a multi-pronged strategy including peer 
counselling and behaviour change; 
• Preventive interventions for the general population through 
programmes for blood safety, voluntary counselling and testing 
services, Prevention of Parent to Child Transmission (PPTCT), 
Information Education and Communication (IEC); 
• Provision of low cost care and support services by providing 
community care services, treatment of opportunistic infections and 
prevention of occupational exposure; 
• Collaborative efforts to promote inter-sectoral programme activities 
including workplace interventions and public private partnerships; 
• Build technical and managerial capacities for programme 
implementation through surveillance, training, monitoring and 
evaluation, technical resource gr oups, operational research and 
programme management.

1191. SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA. Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India has the World's highest incidence of 
cancer of the gall bladder, mouth and lower pharynx; 
157 

RAJYA SABHA [11 March, 2005] 
(b) whether it is also a fact that accord ing to a report, thyroid cancer has 
been detected in women in the coastal districts of Kerala, Karnataka and Goa; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that said report had highlighted and confirmed 
earlier observation that the breast cance r has replaced cervical cancer as the 
leading site of cancer among women in Indian cities and that lung cancer is 
the common cancer in various metropolitan cities in the country; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and the action Government propose to 
reduce the changing risk of cancer? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) 
According to the Cancer Atlas brought out by Indian Council of Medical 
Research (ICMR) based on data collected under the National Cancer Registry 
Programme (NCRP), the incidence of different cancers is not uniform 
throughout the country. While cancer inci dence in India as a whole is much 
lower in comparison to the incidence across the world, the incidence cancers 
of mouth, tongue and gall bladder in the country is higher than those reported 
in the "Cancer Incidence of 5 Continents" published by WHO in 2002. As per 
the Atlas on the basis of ICMR's population based cancer registry data, the 
highest incidence rates have been reported for the cancer of gall bladder 
among the women in Delhi and the cancer of tongue and mouth among the 
men in Bhopal. The highest rate of cancer of lower Pharynx as reported from 
Aizwal is based on the inputs from the Collaborative Centres which include 
private hospitals as well. 
(b) According to the Cancer Atlas, th yroid cancer has been detected in the 
coastal areas of Kerala, Karnataka and Goa. Breast cancer among women is 
one of the leading cancers in urban areas  whereas lung cancer is not the most 
common cancer in the Metropolitan cities in India. 
In order to control this problem, National Cancer Control programme was 
launched in 1975 with the objectives  of prevention, early detection and 
treatment of cancer in the country. The strategies under the program me are 
awareness generation in the community for prevention and early detection of 
cancer, and provision of comprehensive cancer treatment facilities across the 
country byway of supporting Regional Cancer Centres. Government Medical 
Colleges and Government Hospitals are also supported by Development of 
Oncology Wings.

rates on steel items and fixation of value caps for all items of iron and steel 
and ferro alloys, increasing allocation of  iron and steel materials for the SSI 
sector and advising steel PSUs to export only after fulfilling the domestic 
requirement.

SPECIAL MENTIONS 
Need to increase the Service Tax Net 
SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA (Andhra Pradesh) : 'Services' constitute a very 
heterogeneous spectrum of economic activities. Over a period of time, the 
definition 'Service' has also undergone a ch ange. In any Welfare State, if is the 
primary responsibility of the Government  to fulfil the increasing developmental 
needs of the country and its people by way of public expenditure. India, being a 
developing economy, is striving to fulfil t he obligations of a Welf are State within its 
limited resources. The service sector is now occupying the centre stage of 
economy; so much so, in the contempora ry world, development of service sector 
has become synonymous with the advancement  of economy. As we know that the 
Government's primary sources of revenue ar e direct and indirect taxes. Apart from 
getting revenue, the Government also wish to raise employment opportunities in 
service sector. With this view, the Gove rnment of India imposed Service Tax on 
some services which cover a range of activities -management, banking, insurance, 
hospitality, administration, communication, entertainment, wholesale distribution 
and retailing including R&D activities. 
196 

[11 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Presently, there are 71 services operating in India. But the Government of 
India has not included services like legal and medial which are available only 
against huge payment, and the Government is not getting any revenue on the 
services rendered by them. Hence I request, that the Government should 
impose Service Tax on the above professions and on similar other professions 
which will help to generate more revenue that can then be used to make this. 
country a welfare State. I also request to have a single window mechanism for 
Service Tax in avoiding computational difficulties. 
Accord of Central Approval for Cauvery Water Supply Scheme for 
Bangalore City 
SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD (Karnataka): Sir, to cope with the growing 
demand in Bangalore Urban conglomeration area, the Government of 
Karnataka has proposed to augment the existing water supply capacity by an 
additional 540 million litres a day, under  the Cauvery Water Supply Scheme 
Stage IV, Phase II. 
Due to erratic monsoons for years in a row and depleting ground 
water resources, it is imperative that a public utility project of this nature and 
magnitude should be in place to cater to the growing demand for potable water

THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RE SOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) and (b) The Centra l Government is empowered by the 
University Grants Commission (UGC) Act, 1956 to notify an institution for 
higher education as a Deemed to be University, on the advice of the UGC. The 
UGC has framed guidelines for consider ing proposals in this regard. These 
guidelines, inter alia, provide that an institution should generally be engaged in 
teaching programmes and research, which are innovative, and of a very high 
academic standard. On being recognised as a Deemed to be University, the 
institution should be capable of further enriching the University system. It 
should be competent to undertake application-oriented programmes in 
emerging areas which are relevant and useful to various development sectors and 
to society in general. While ordinarily, an institution should have been in 
existence for 10 years with infrastructure as prescribed by the relevant 
statutory bodies monitoring standards of education; those imparting education in 
the emerging areas with the promise of excellence can be considered for a 
provisional status of Deemed to be University under the 'de-novo' category. 
(c) to (e) According to the UGC seven proposals are pending for a decision by the 
Commission. A Screening Committee has been constituted for expediting 
disposal of proposals as and when they are received. A Review Committee has also 
been constituted to consider representation against the decision of the Screening 
Committee. The Central Advisory Board of Education (CABE) has constituted a 
Committee to consider issues impinging on autonomy of Universities and other 
higher education institutions.

*175.    SHRI B. J. PANDA: 
SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: 
Will the Minister of CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Govern ment propose to preserve and 
propagate various Indian folk music forms in the shape of Lok Tarang; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the action plan to popularize this concept with a view to make it a 
marketable medium and sideline the movie songs? 
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) In January, every year all the Seven Zonal Cultural Centres (ZCCs) 
organise "National Folk Dance Festival" as part of Republic Day 
Celebrations. From this year it was decided to call this dance festival, of which 
folk music forms are an integral pa rt, "Lok Tarang". "Lok Tarang" gives a 
platform to folk artists from across the country to perform annually at the 
National Capital. 
(c) To popularize this concept the Lok Tarang festival was documented as a 
joint effort of all the ZCCs located in seven different parts of the country. A 
CD of folk songs prepared by the Eastern Zonal Cultural Centre comprising of folk 
songs from all over India was released on the occasion in an effort to popularize 
folk music amongst the masses. 
The ZCCs are involved in promoting and propagating folk art forms through 
various schemes like Guru Shishya Parampara, Theatre Rejuvenation, National 
Cultural Exchange Programme etc.

*177. SHRI SANJAY NIRUPAM: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have proposed tools to fix problem of delay in justice 
delivery; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the estimated cost to implement the 
proposal; 
(c) whether Government have also set up any monitoring authority to watch 
the progress of the reforms; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): (a) 
Pendency of cases in various layers of Judiciary is due to several complex factors. 
In order to reduce pendency of cases Government has initiated a number of 
measures which include, timely filling up of the vacancies of judges, increasing 
the judge strength, grouping of cases involving common questions of law, 
constitution of specialized benches, organizing LokAdalats at regular intervals, 
encouraging alternative modes of dispute resolution like negotiation, mediation and 
arbitration and setting up of special tribunals like Central Administrative Tribunals, 
State Administrative Tribunals, Income Tax Appellate Tribunals, Family Courts and 
Labour Courts. 
Further it has been decided to focus on  reforms in a few core areas which 
include computerization of judiciary, disposal through fast track courts, 
development of physical infrastructure, and evolution of strategies to cope with 
massive governance related inadquacies in Indian judiciary through studies, 
pilots and reform projects. 
(b) Remedial measures for pendency of cases in the Judiciary cannot be 
quantified in cost. However the proposed cost of computerization of 13,348 
District and Subordinate Courts in Rs. 384.52 crore. 
(c) and (d) The progress of the reforms is being monitored at various levels 
of the Government.

(a) whether any system has been evolved for speedy disposal of the cases 
pertaining to the senior citizens, disabled persons, retired

Government personnel and socially oppressed persons and provide them legal 
assistance in the High Courts and the Supreme Court; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the High Courts where this system has been implemented; and

THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): (a) to 
(d) Priority is being accord ed for speedy disposal of cases relating to senior 
citizens, disabled persons and atrocities on women. In the year 1999, the 
Chief Justice of India wrote to the Chief Justices of all High Courts to identify 
and dispose of matters on priority basis in which persons above 65 years of age 
were involved. More recently the Union Government has impressed on Chief 
Ministers of States and the Chief Justices of High Courts to earmark one Fast Track 
Court, where there are more than one to deal exclusively with cases involving 
senior citizens. Similarly, instructions have been issued that all cases relating to 
women, particularly those arising out of sexual abuse and cruelties in marriage 
may be assigned to one of Fast Track Courts at the district level for their 
speedy disposal. The Government has also requested the High Courts to accord 
priority to the cases in which persons with 40 per cent or more disability as 
per the Disability Act are involved in litigation. 
Most of the High Courts have issued instructions for according priority for 
disposal of cases relating to senior citizens and abuse of women. These, 
inter-alia, include High Courts of Allahabad, Bombay, Calcutta, Guwahati, 
Gujarat, Jharkhand, Orissa, Madras, Punjab, and Haryana, Rajasthan, Sikkim 
and Uttaranchal and Govt, of Meghalaya and Tripura. 
The scheme for providing legal aid to disabled persons and other weaker sections 
of the society such as Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, has already been 
evolved and implemented under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987. All 
these categories are entitled to free legal aid and services. These can be availed 
through High Court Legal Services Committees functioning under each High 
Court in the country. In case the matter is before the Supreme Court of India 
free legal services can be

As regards Supreme Court, matters relating to Senior Citizens of the age 
from 65 onwards have been included in the Terminal List of 2004 to be given

to which they belong are listed within 15 working days from the date of their 
registration. The Supreme Court Legal Service Committee and the Supreme 
Court Middle Income Group Legal Aid Society have been providing legal aid 
free of cost to litigants and socially oppressed persons subject to satisfying the 
eligibility criteria prescribed in this regard.

Protected monuments 
1240.SHRI V. HANUMANTHA RAO: Will the Minister of CULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the number of protected monuments, presently on the list maintained by the 
Archaeological Survey of India; 
(b) the criteria to be fulfilled by any monument to come under this category; 
(c) whether there is a constant review of such needs by Governments; 
(d) to what extent the ASI has been able to extend protection to the valuable 
monuments; and 
(e) what steps the ASI proposes to take to enhance the number of such monuments? 
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) 
Archaeological Survey of India protects and maintains 3658 monuments/ sites declared 
to be of national importance. 
(b) Under Section 4 of the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains 
Act, 1958, ancient monuments which are of historical, archaeological or artistic 
interest and which have been in existence for not 
60 

[14 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
less then 100 years are declared as monuments of national importance through 
notification in the official gazette of India. 
(c) Yes, Sir. Protection of monuments/sites is a continuous process and the 
proposals received from field offices and various other agencies are examined 
on the merit of each case and if such proposals fulfill the criteria laid down as 
per the provisions of Ancient Monuments, Archaeological Sites and Remains 
Act, 1958, they are considered for protection after obtaining approval of the 
competent authority. 
(d) The Archaeological Survey of I ndia has an annual conservation 
programme for the protected monuments and sites. This includes continuous 
assessment of the state of preservation, taking up required civil works and 
chemcial preservation. Apart from th e above, the Archaeological Survey of 
India extends physical protection to the monuments and sites declared to be of 
national importance through the deployment of its watch and ward staff, 
private security guards, state police and/or C.I.S.F depending on the needs of 
each monument. 
(e) As stated at (c) above, the need for extending central protection is 
constantly being reviewed. 
During the last five years 59 monuments/sites were added to the list of 
monuments and sites of national importance.

1257. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD:  Will the Minister of HUMAN

country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) to (c) The 
Government of India in collaboration with the United Nations Office of Drugs and 
Crime conducted a national survey on extent, pattern and trends and drug abuse 
in India. The age group of the sample survey was between 
74 

[14 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
12 to 60 years. As per the survey the prevalence of drug use in sample size of 
8,587 within 12 to 18 years age group was as follows: 
Cannabis      3.0% 
Opiates        0.1% 
Since students at secondary and higher secondary level are vulnerable to drug 
abuse due to stress, peer influence, hormonal changes etc., educating them on 
the ill-effects of the drug abuse through appropriate inputs in school curricula 
has been taken up. The NCERT has developed a General Framework of 
Adolescence Education with drug abuse as one of the major components. The 
Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment is the nodal Ministry for prevention 
of alcoholism and substance abuse. That Ministry also funds voluntary 
organisation that are running awareness programmes in the area of drug abuse 
prevention. Those organisations cover schools and colleges under their outreach 
programmes. Besides, to check the peddling of the drugs to students, the sale of 
such substance in the vicinity of any school/educational institution attracts 
higher than the minimum punishment for such offence.

Three language formula 
†1280. SHRI R.S. GAVAI: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the three language formula adopted by the S.S.C. 
and H.S.C. for its examinations has become insignificant; 
(b) if so, whether Government are considering to drop it; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor and the steps being taken by Government to get 
this formula adopted by the boards of all the States? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) to (d) The Three 
Language Formula as advocated by National Policy on Education was approved 
by the Parliament. The Formula is applicable at the upper primary stage and has to 
continue upto the end of secondary stage i.e. Class X. This formula provides 
for a study of the mother tongue or the regional language compulsory as the 
first language. It also requires the study of Hindi, English and a modern Indian 
language, preferably one of the Southern languages in the Hindi speaking States, 
Hindi and English in the non-Hindi speaking States. The National Curriculum 
Framework for School Education (NCFSE) 2000 of the National Council of 
Educational Research and Training (NCERT) has also included the provisions 
of the Three Language Formula. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
93 

RAJYA SABHA [14 March, 2005] 
This formula, which flows from a policy decision, is to be reflected in the 
school curriculum. The role of the Central Government in the matter of the 
Implementation of the formula is recommendatory. The implementation of the 
Three Language Formula is the sole responsibility of the State Governments. 
All the States/Union Territories had, accordingly, been urged by the Government 
from time to time to implement it. While all the schools affiliated to the Central 
Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) and the Council for the Indian School 
Certificate Examination (CISCE) have already implemented it, most of the 
States/UTs, too, are implementing this formula.

Crime Based Programmes on TV Channels 
† 1298. DR. CHHATTRAPAL SINGH LODHA: 
SHRIMATIMAYAS'INGH:  
SHRI JAYANTILAL BAROT: 
Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government are going to take any specific steps to exercise control 
on the news related to crimes, violence, obscenity on television channels; 
(b) Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) the number of accused involved in  criminal incidents who have 
admitted to be influenced by such programmes in the last six months? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. 
JAIPAL REDDY): (a) and (b) Programmes telecast on TV channels 
transmitted/retransmitted through the cable television network are required to adhere 
to the Programme Code prescribed under the Cable Television Networks 
(Regulation) Act, 1995 and Rules framed thereunder. The Programme Code, 
inter alia, provides that no programmes should be carried in the cable service 
which— 
* Is likely to encourage or incite violence or contains anything against 
maintenance of law and order or which promotes anti-national 
attitudes; 
* Contravenes the provisions of the Cinematograph Act, 1952; 
* Is not suitable for unrestricted public exhibition. 
The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting held a Workshop on content issues 
on television channels on 16th February, 2005 with stakeholders, media heads, 
NGOs, cable operators associations, etc. One of the recommendations was 
that there should be time of the day slotting for programmes especially those with 
content not suitable for universal viewing. Government is considering the setting up of 
a regulatory authority to regulate the content on TV channels.

Portrayal of Gods in advertisements 
†1301. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: Will the Minister of INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that advertisements are being exhibited 
where Hindu Gods are being portrayed in ridiculous manner; 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
111 

RAJYA SABHA [14 March, 2005] 
(b) if so, whether Government have given liberty for this; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the action taken by Government against the persons responsible for it? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. 
JAIPAL REDDY): (a) to (d) Press in India enjoys constitutional freedom. The 
Press Council of India (PCI) is a statutory body established for preserving the freedom 
of the Press and for maintaining and improving the standards of newspapers and 
news agencies in India. PCI has set the Norms for Journalistic Ethics according 
to which newspapers/journals shall not publish anything which has a tendency to 
malign or hurt the religious sentiments of any community or any section of 
society. 
Doordarshan and All India Radio follow their own Codes for commercial 
advertising, which do not allow anything to be shown that hurt the religious 
sentiments of the people. The adver tisements of all TV channels when 
transmitted/retransmitted through the cable network are required to adhere to the 
Advertising Code prescribed under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) 
Act, 1995 and Rules framed thereunder. The Advertising Code inter alia prohibits 
advertisements, which contain references that hurt religious sentiments and 
which offend religious susceptibilities. 
The Central Government has constituted an inter-ministerial committee under 
Section 20 of the aforesaid Act to look into the violation of the Advertising Code. 
Cognizance of such violation of Advertising Code is also taken suo . moto by the 
Committee. No complaint about any such advertisement, on any TV channel has 
been brought to the notice of the Government. 
The Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) certifies films, including that 
of advertisements for public exhibition under the provisions of Section 5(B) of the 
Cinematograph Act, 1952 and the guidelines framed there under. While certifying 
the advertisements it is ensured that no visuals or words contemptuous of racial, 
religious or other groups are shown.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI K. 
VENKATAPATHY): (a) Due to the huge pendency of cases at High Court and 
subordinate court levels, the number of Judges appear inadequate. 
The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in its judgement of 21st March, 2002, in All India 
Judges'Association & Ors. Vs. Union of India & Ors., had directed that an increase in the 
Judge strength from the existing 10.5 or 13 per 10 lakh people to 50 judges per 10 lakh 
people should be effected and implemented within a period of five years in a phased 
manner to be determined and directed by the Union Ministry of Law. The Court, had also 
directed that the existing vacancies in the Subordinate courts at all levels should be filled. 
The Central Government have filed an affidavit in the Supreme Court praying that the 
increase in judge strength in the Union Territories for which the Central Government is 
administratively responsible be allowed based on workload and pendency of cases. The 
matter is sub-judice. 
Under article 235 of the Constitution of India, the administrative control over the 
members of subordinate judiciary in the States vests with the concerned High Court 
and the State Government. Thus as regards increase in judge strength in the District 
and subordinate courts and filling up of the vacant posts, the primary responsibility 
for taking necessary action vests with the respective State Governments. All the State 
Governments are also party to the above mentioned All India Judges Case. 
At High Court level, the last Triennial Review of the Judge strength of the various 
High Courts were held in 2003. As a result, it was decided to increase the Judge strength of 
various High Courts from the existing strength of 655 to 749 Judges, subject to the State 
Governments agreeing to meet the cost of increased strength.

1351. SHRI PENUMALLI MADHU: Will the Minister of TRIBAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether tribals evicted from 1.52 lakh hectares of forest land upto the 
31st March 2004, are entitled to any compensation, land rights and 
rehabilitation packages;

159

that they are compensated and their rights are acquired? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH): (a) to (d) 
The Ministry of Environment and Forests have informed that encroachment on 
forest lands is a serious offence under Section 26 of the Indian Forest Act, 1927. 
Therefore, in conformity with the law, the ineligible encroachers have to be 
evicted from the forest lands and are as such not entitled to compensation 
under the Indian Forest Act. In pursuance of the Hon'ble Supreme Court's 
order dated 23.11.2001 in Writ Petition (C) No. 202 of 1995, the Central 
Government instructed all the State/UT Governments on 3rd May 2002 to evict 
ineligible encroachers from forest lands in a time bound manner. Since then, as 
per information received from the State/UT Governments till 31.03.2004, 
ineligible encroachers including tribal people have been evicted from 1.52 lakh 
hectares of forest lands. At the same time, 3.65 lakh hectares of pre 1980 
encroachments of eligible people on forest land have been regularized and 384 
forest villages covering an area of 0.34 lakh hectares have been converted into 
revenue villages.

THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT (SHRI GHULAM NABI 
AZAD): (a) and (b) As per Entry 5 of the State List of the Constitution, 
'municipality' is a State subject. In view of this, it is for the State Government to see

175 

RAJYA SABHA [14 March, 2005] 
State/Municipality regarding encroachment of functional domain of 
municipalities. 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) As stated in the reply to part (a) & (b), 'Municipality' is a State subject. 
In view of this, it is for the State Governments to take necessary steps in 
augmenting financial resources of the municipalities and assisting them to come 
out of the financial stress, thereby improving their fiscal position. The 
Government of India have, however, taken initiatives to help urban local bodies 
come out of their fiscal stress. These include: 
 
* Urban Reforms Incentive Fund to provide reform-linked assistance to states. 
* Tax-free Municipal Bonds for issue by urban local bodies for potable water 
supply, severage or sanitation, drainage, solid waste management, 
roads/bridges/flyovers, and urban transport. In addition, the Central 
Government has announced tax exemption in case of bonds issued by 
municipal/local Governments for raising resources for urban 
infrastructure. 
* Public-Private Participation Guide lines have been issued for providing 
directions to States and municipalities to manage the process of 
involving the private sector in water supply and sanitation sector. 
* Property Tax Guidelines have been issued in 1998 to all State 
Governments with the objective of simplification and rationalization of 
property tax, which is considered as  one of the best source of revenue 
for the urban local bodies. 
* A Model Municipal Law has been  circulated to States for 
implementation of its provisions that include provision for enhanced 
borrowing, allowing entry of private sector, authorising concessionaires to 
penalize user for non-payment of tariffs, etc. 
* The States have been requested to implement the report of the Task Force 
constituted by the Office of C & AG of India to recommend accounting 
and budget formates for urban local  bodies. The Task force report 
recommends accrual based accounting system. This system would 
facilitate urban local bodies to access private capital markets. 
176 

[14 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Besides the above, the support provided by the Government of India 
through Centrally Sponsored/Central Sector Schemes, viz. Integrated 
Development of Small and Medium Towns (IDSMT), Infrastructural 
Development in Mega Cities, Acceler ated Urban Water Supply Programme 
(AUWSP) and Research in Urban and Regional Planning, help the State 
Governments in their endeavour to strengthen the urban local bodies. 
The Central Finance Commission also devolves funds upon the 
municipalities through the State Governments for operation and maintenance 
of core municipal services. The Eleventh Finance Commission have devolved a 
grant of Rs. 2,000 crores for the above purpose for the period 2000-05.

Steps to increase Urban Employment 
1381. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR S ANGHI: Will the Minister of URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any concrete efforts have been made during the last five years 
to increase the urban employment particul arly in major cities like Hyderabad 
etc.; and 
(b) if so, the complete details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARISELJA): (a) and 
(b) The Ministry of Urban Employment and Poverty Alleviation has been 
implementing a Centrally sponsored Employment Oriented Urban Poverty 
Alleviation Programme named Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana 
(SJSRY), on all India basis, including the major cities of the country through 
States/Union Territories, with effect from 01.12.1997 with a view to providing 
gainful employment to the urban unemployed and underemployed poor 
through, firstly, encouraging the setting up of self-employment ventures by those 
who have studied upto 9th standard and, secondly, by providing 
183 

RAJYA SABHA [14 March, 2005] 
wage employment by utilizing their labour for construction of socially and 
economically useful public assets. The scheme is funded in the ratio of 75:25 
between the Centre and the States. 
Under SJSRY, State-wise data are received at the Central level in Ministry of 
Urban Employment and Poverty Alleviation, through the Quarterly Progress 
Reports received from the States/UTs. 
In the State of Andhra Pradesh, since inception of SJSRY total 1,31,145 persons 
have been assisted to set up micro en terprises for self-employment and 35,894 
persons have been provided skill training. Under the wage employment 
component, 88.48 lakh mandays of work have been generated in the Andhra 
Pradesh.

Environment and Forests was created by Shri Rajiv Gandhi in 1985. It is directly 
responsible for the implementation of the Wildlife Protection Act (WRA), Forest 
Conservation Act (FCA), Environment Protection Act (EPA) and the recent 
Biodiversity Act-the States are the implementing agencies. 
206 

[14 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
In 2005, twenty years after it was created, it has become a Khichdi of 
hundreds of different things. Forests, wildlife and the environment are all 
part of a single department. Forest protection, conservation of all the wildlife 
in it, maintaining ecologically fragile areas and governing institutions for 
research, like the Indian Council fo r Forest Research and Education 
(ICFRE), Botanical Survey of India (BSI), Zoological Survey of India (ZSI), 
Wildlife Institute of India (Wll), river cleaning operations, afforestation of 
land, coastal regulation Zones, eco-development, environmental research 
and education, the huge national River Conservation Directorate, hazardous 
substance management, pollution control boards, clean technologies, water 
quality monitoring, fly ash utilisation,  climate change, externally aided 
projects, animal welfare matters, administration of zoos and global 
conventions are all part of the responsibilities of this Ministry. 
Thus, the Ministry of Environment  and Forests is burdened with 
innumerable activities with no connection to quality or content. The present 
structure and functioning of the Ministry of Environment and Forests is 
unacceptable. It needs to be sliced into two-a Ministry of Environment and 
a Ministry of Forests. I request the hon. Prime Minister to act quickly. 
Otherwise, the entire machinery that governs our natural world will remain 
stagnant and it would be a huge invitation to more nature disasters.

Need for A Comprehensive Review of the Company Law to stop 
Fraudulent Practices by Promoters of Companies 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRA IAH (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, my Special 
Mention pertains to corporate governance in the country. I wish to draw 
the attention of the Government to  the issues related to corporate 
governance. The growth of the corporate sector in the country is critically 
dependent on the environment of the capital markets. Equally important is 
to protect the interests of the investors. There have been several instances 
when unscrupulous promoters have made attempts to defraud investors. 
There is also the issue of vanishing companies. The number of vanishing 
companies, as on November, 2004, was 115, These companies had floated 
public issues and mopped up funds to the tune of Rs. 803 crores. 
The Securities Exchange Board of India is the regulator of the capital 
market in this country. In addition, the Government also has to play a key 
role in preventing such instances. Although the Department of Company 
Affairs has taken a number of steps ov er the last few years, yet a lot 
needs to be done. 
209 

RAJYA SABHA [14 March, 2005] 
There is also a need to have a comprehensive review of the Company 
Law in the wake of the developments in capital markets—both in India and 
globally. It is necessary to incorporate stringent punitive measures in the 
legislation so that action can be initiated under the Company Law and 
also under various provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code. 
-   This would enable the SEBI to take more stringent action against 
vanishing and defaulting companies. 
There have been several instances, where large, reputed companies 
have generated huge amounts of capital through various debt and equity 
schemes only to later file for bankruptcy. In the final analysis, it is the 
small investors, who have lost their hard-earned money, even while not 
much action has been taken against the promoters of these companies. 
Therefore, I request the Government to take a serious note of the situation, 
and appropriate action has to be taken so that small investors are protected.

Demand for establishment of a Regional Neonatal Care Centre in 
West Bengal 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA(West Bengal): Thank you very much, 
Sir. My Special Mention pertains to  a very serious matter of national 
importance because child mortality is a very serious problem in our country. 
Even the UNDP also rates us very low. So, my Special Mention pertains to 
establishment of a Regional Neonatal Care Centre in West Bengal. 
Even after almost six decades of independence, our country faces the 
biggest newborn health challenge in the entire community of nations. Every 
year, unfortunately, India accounts for 30 per cent of neonatal deaths world 
over. As many as 12 lakh newborn die during the first four weeks of life. 
This might seem to be an insurmountable challenge to confront with. A 
serious contributing factor for such death of newborns is the perennial 
problem of low birth weight i.e., birth weight below 2500 gms, mostly due 
to poor prenatal care and rampant malnutrition of mothers. More than 30 
per cent of country's new newborn babies weigh less than a normal child, 
and it leads to about 65 per cent neonatal deaths. Hence, depending on 
the birth weight, the baby should be referred to particular level of care for 
210 

[14 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
optimum results. Thus, while the community-based care centres in States 
are to operate; at the same time, a regional centre, dedicated to the care 
of new born, is also an absolute necessity. A scientific neonatal care 
training must also be imparted to the health care providers in order to fight 
the problem. The aim of such Regional Neonatal Care Centres should also 
be to search innovative methods fo r implementing and improving the 
newborn care in that region. Such centres should also aim to provide other 
essential facilities, like neonatal cardiology, surgery, ophthalmology (ROP), 
etc. It is satisfying that the northern, the Southern and the Western parts 
of India has such centres. But they should be further augmented because 
they are not in proper shape. And, there must be, at least, one fully equipped 
centre in Eastern India, preferably in West Bengal. I am sure the House 
will join me on this score.

Sir, I thank you for permitting me to raise this issue once again.Through 
my Special Mention made during the last session, I had requested for an 
amendment of article 371 of the Constitution with reference to Karnataka. 
However, there is no significant progress on the issue. I am, therefore, 
appealing for making an amendment again. 
Due to certain factors, Hyderabad, Karnataka, including the districts of 
Bidar, Gulbarga, Bellary, Koppal, Raichur, Bijapur, Bagalkotetc, have not 
been able to keep pace with the rest of the State in terms of Comprehensive 
Composite Development Index, including education and per capita income.

RAJYA SABHA [14 March, 2005] 
Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, following intense unrest over inter-regional 
disparity, the Karnataka Legislat ive Assembly unanimously passed a 
resolution requesting the Centre to amend article 371 to enable the 
Karnataka Government to provide for regional reservation in the State in 
the matter of emptoyment and education to overcome the regional imbalance 
and for overall development of the region. 
Under similar circumstances of regional imbalance within a State, the 
Centre amended article 371 for development of certain backward regions 
in some States, including Andhra Pradesh. However, with regard to the

Sir, in the background of serious problems in the Indian Railways, with the 
problems of railway safety, lack of passenger amenities, the lapses of 
Indian Railways in many other areas, we welcome this Budget. This Budget 
is better when compared to many other Budgets presented in recent times 
by various Railway Ministers. Our party welcome this Budget because of 
the fact that in the present Budget there is no hike on the passenger fare. 
There is no freight hike even on many items. Even in the last Budget, there 
was no hike in passenger fare. 
Sir, I could not find any programme in the present Budget with regard to 
electrification. I don't know what is the programme of the Indian Railways 
with regard to electrification. Though the electrification of the Indian Railways 
started way back in 1925, as per the figures of 2004, only 27 per cent of 
the Indian Railways is electrified. I have not seen the Railway Minister 
saying to that. I wanted to know as to what is the programme he has on 
electrification? How is the programme going to be implemented? It is a 
very important programme because it reduces India's dependence on diesel 
which we are importing now. Besides, it is an eco-friendly system. This is 
a very important point. I want to know from the hon. Railway Minister. 
Electrification should not be a programme for two or three or four years. 
So, I would like to know about the thinking of the Indian Railways on this. 
Sir, in the Budget Estimates we find that there is some improvement. 
There is an increase in the passenger receipts as well. In 2004-05, the 
Budget Estimateswere Rs. 13,940 cr ores and the Revised Estimates 
were Rs. 14,035 crores. So, there was an increase of Rs. 95 crores. If we 
compare the passenger receipts of 2003-04, it stood at Rs. 13,620 crores 
in the Budget Estimates and the Revised Estimates were Rs. 13,298 
crores. So, there was a shortfall of about Rs. 322 crores. And, in 2004-05,

crores, but the revised figure is Rs. 2819.05 crores. So, in the upper class 
passenger fare there was a shortfall of Rs. 407.31 crores against the 
estimated budgeted figure. So, taking many things into consideration, like

SHRIMATI BIMBA RAIKAR (Karnataka): Sir, the railway is the most 
common and economical mode of transport in India. A vast network of 
railway serves every nook and comer of the country as a binding force in 
national integration. 
In his current Railway Budget, the hon. Railway Minister has not touched 
upon any new revision in fares and freights. The railway needs to provide 
for increasing costs of fuel or power, and, also of salary, wages and pension 
liabilities of a big workforce. In addition, it was also necessary to provide 
for adequate allocations for on-going doubling and gauge conversion 
projects, and, also for new projects just announced in this Budget. People 
are now used to bear extra expenses in the form of increased prices of 
sugar, petrol, LPG and diesel as also of cosmetics, cellphone bills etc. 
Compared to other public transport, the bus, the railway offers the cheapest 
option for travel. For instance, the bus fare in the ordinary class from 
Bangalore to Belgaum in Karnataka comes to around Rs. 180, and, in 
case of deluxe bus, you have to pay Rs. 250 to Rs. 300. But, in an 
unreserved second class, you pay less than Rs. 80/- to cover this distance. 
Therefore, unlike daily consumptio n items, people would have gladly 
accepted an increase in railway fare as they travel once in a while and not 
almost daily. 
Increase in passenger or freight fares is the only way to mop up additional 
funds to substantial extent. Instead of this, attempts have been made on 
piecemeal basis, and, by cutting corners, that is, cost reduction, which 
result in saving only meagre funds. The Centre is not going to provide 
larger budgetary support to railways, as it wants railways to manage its 
affairs and finances better and generate own reserves. 
Railway finances revolved around cross-subsidy. For every rupee earned, 
sixty-five paise comes from freight earnings. Another fifteen paise comes 
from upper class fare earnings. The fare earnings from lower class 
passengers account only for fifteen paise per rupee earned. The lower 
class passengers constitute around eighty five per cent of total travellers, 
and, therefore, heavily subsidised. Now, the Minister has announced 
concessions to students, job app licants and kisans. The incidence of 
subsidy has increased which is eating into freight and upper class fare 
earnings. The Railway Minister's philosophy seems to be that if you don't 
pay more, you cannot ask for more in safety, amenities and comfort in

concessions and not sportspersons, who are, on the average, very affluent. 
A major share of operational expens es goes for payment of diesel/ 
power, the cost of which is increasing day by day. Added to this is the 
pension liabilities for which no reserve provision has been made as

accept coal freight only on prepayment by the SEBs and the NTPC.

25 per cent of total requirements of wagons. The movement of bulk 
commodities like coal, fertilisers, cement and foodgrains (for FCI Public

national highway improvement projects are underway and the road transport

movement. A decade ago, the Railways used to carry 68 per cent of total

stiff competition by road transport sector.

which are going to make some difference to the way the Railway Ministry 
is being run. 
The first point I want to emphasise is that given the current importance 
of infrastructure, we must recognise that the Railways are probably the 
most important infrastructure sector that we have. We do not hear much 
about it, except at the time of the annual Budget. But from the connectivity 
point of view, it is the most important; it is more important even than roads. 
Roads are important. But for long distance connectivity, it is the most 
important. For most of the people of our country, it is the most important 
means of long distance transport. But we have not done as much as we 
should have done. I think this has come out that there is lot more to be 
done. So, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, the two important points that I wanted 
to make essentially are; one, that if we want to give the highest importance 
to the Railways as we should, to use a phrase which has emanated from 
the Prime Minister, I believe, that you have to do some "out-of-the-box" 
thinking, almost what needs to be done in the Railways. 
My first suggestion is that you cannot solve or resolve the problems of 
the Railways through this annual budgeting processes. You need a 
programme at least - not the type of a Five Year Plan that we have for 
different sectors - of five year of massive investment in the railway sector. 
That can be done because today we have the resources, we have the 
ability and we have the skill, this is the oldest enterprise of which we can 
be proud of If we have a five year programme of investments with specific 
proposals where the investments are going, in terms of safety, in terms of 
expansion, in terms of track renewal and so on and so forth. We know 
what needs to be done. But we need a five year approach. This has to be 
beyond what we normally do in terms of the Planning Commission, which 
provides outlays, and says all the right things and annual plans, which 
also say the right things. 
The related suggestion, Sir, is that this annual budget, to my mind, is 
rather meaningless. I mean that it is 150 years old enterprise; you do not 
have annual budget for aviation or annual budget for roads or annual budget 
for any other sector. But you have annual Railway Budget and this is an 
265 

RAJYA SABHA [14 March, 2005] 
anachronism. This is probably a hangover from the British days. One 
suggestion, I know it would not be accepted because everybody likes the 
high media profile but I have to make this suggestion that if you want to 
make a difference to the Railways, then you have to move away from the 
business of regarding budget as something very different from the budget 
for any other most important sectors of our economy. So, this is the first 
suggestion - massive investments,a five year programme of investments 
by the Railways for the Railways, for the people of India, broken into physical 
annual segments about which an annu al report can be presented to 
Parliament and the annual report can be discussed. That is what we will 
be discussing and not the kind of discussion whether the fares should be 
increased by one per cent or two per cent or three per cent. So this is my 
first suggestion. I know it won't be easy to implement. The second 
suggestion, which is also more difficult from the political point of view, is 
essentially that you need to create a distance between administration and 
policy making. There is no basic, fundamental reason that if you want to 
make the Railways the best in the world, the Railway Board has to located 
in the Railway Ministry. I can think of  no other public enterprise of this 
importance, which is located in a Ministry. So you have to demarcate the 
administration which will be the Railway Board, whatever you call it and 
the policy making which can be with the Ministry. If you move away from 
the Annual Budget, frieght charges, fare charges etc. should be left to the 
Administration. The Civil Aviation Ministry or the Road Transport Ministry 
does not decide what the toll rate should be or what the fare should be 
from X to Y to Z. So these decisions should be made by the administrators 
and the Ministry can do the investment decisions and it can make an 
massive difference. I believe that you need to subsidise. You need cross 
subsidisation. I believe in that. But ministry should provide direct subsidies 
through the Budget. We should also provide direct support for investment 
through the Budget. We should monitor the progress of what we are doing 
from year to year and we can debate it in the Parliament. But, I think, we 
have to move away from annual budgeting and we have to move away from 
this integration of administration system with the Ministry. It is complete 
anachronism, which was probably valid, maybe, 40 years ago, 50 years 
ago, but no longer.

move away from annual Budget and create a distance between the Ministry

Benefits of VAT 
*186. SHRI DARA SINGH: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government have fully asse ssed benefits or disadvantages by 
VAT's introduction in the country from 1st April, 2005 and how far it is 
different from Central Sales Tax: 
(b) which are the States who have passed a VAT law till date and whether 
any State not willing to do so; 
(c) whether VAT will operate on the basis of uniform rates across the 
country by ending several State-level or vary in respect of unwilling State 
like Uttar Pradesh; and 
(d) what special relief small dealer s/traders will get under VAT whose 
turnover is up to 5 to 50 lakhs annually? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (d) 
VAT is a State level tax reform measure, which is proposed to be 
implemented by States in lieu of the existing Sales Tax system. An 
Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers has been set up to decide 
on all issues relating to implementation of State Level VAT. The Empowered 
44 

[15 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Committee of State Finance Ministers has decided to implement VAT and 
has finalized the VAT design, after prolonged deliberations and due 
consideration of advantages offered by the VAT System. The State Level 
VAT being introduced from 1st April, 20 05 is different from Central Sales 
Tax, in the sense that while the former is on inter-State sales (i.e. sales within 
a State), the latter is on inter-State sales. 
A statement indicating the latest position with respect to the VAT 
Legislations of States/UTs is give n in the statement-l (See below). No 
State/UT has communicated its unwillingness to pass VAT Legislation. 
As decided by the Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers, 
VAT will operate on the basis of uniform rates across the country. However, 
in case any State is not able to impl ement VAT w.e.f. 1st April, 2005, the 
existing system of sales tax shall continue in that State. Further, as decided 
by the Empowered Committee, it is expected that a number of State level 
taxes on purchase or sales of goods like state sales tax, turnover tax, purchase 
tax, additional sales tax, surcharge, entr y tax (not in lieu of octroi) etc. will 
be subsumed in VAT. 
Small dealers with annual turnover not exceeding Rs. 50 lakhs, who are 
otherwise liable to pay VAT, shall have the option for a compaistion scheme 
with payment of tax at a small percentage to turnover.

Appreciation of Rupee 
*188. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that rupee has appreciated considerably in relation 
to US $ during the past few months; 
(b) if so, the factors responsible for the same; and 
(c) its financial implications on the Indian economy? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) and (b) 
The Rupee appreciated against the US Dollar by 6.1 per cent during the 
period September-February 2004-05. This appreciation has primarily been on 
account to higher supply of foreign ex change, compared to demend, arising 
out of foreign portfolio inflows, trade remittances, etc. against the backdrop 
of the weakness exhibited by US Dollar agaisnt other major currencies in the 
international market. 
(c) The movements in the Rupee value have been smooth and orderly, 
avoiding any significant costs to the economy. Both exports and imports have 
continued to post robust growth and, coupled with strong capital inflows, the 
overall balance of payments position remains comfortable. The foreign 
exchange reserves,which stood at US $ 113 billion at end-March 2004, have 
improved further, and are currently placed at US $ 135.7 billion, as on 
February, 25.2005.

Strategic Stock of Petroleum 
†*191. SHRI P.K. MAHESWARI: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have withdrawn the scheme of setting up of a 
strategic stock of petroleum on the pattern of America and China; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have also suspended the scheme of raising price 
stabilization fund of petroleum products; and 
(d) the reasons for suspending the both schemes? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLUEM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI 
MANI SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) and (b) Government propose to build 
strategic storage of crude oil for storing 5 million metric tonne of crude oil. 
The proposed storage would be in addition to the existing storage of crude 
oil and petroleum products with the oil companies and would provide an 
emergency response mechanism to any sudden or severe oil supply 
disruptions. 
(c) and (d) Government have approved a Price Band Method of pricing 
for petrol and diesel, which has an inbuilt mechanism to allow variations in 
product prices in tandem with import pa rity prices within a floor and ceiling 
price. As the price band itself takes care of the problems which would 
otherwise have had to be addressed by a stabilization mechanism, the 
stabilization fund proposal is not being pursued for the moment in the 
expectation that the prices band mechanism would be restored once 
international oil prices stabilize.

have been eased.

particular to small borrowers, banks have been advised that they may waive

sectoral cap and also complies with prescribed pricing guidelines.

Introduction of VAT in the country 
1462. SHRI CHO.S. RAMASWAMY: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Go vernment are intr oducing the VAT 
system all over the country from April, 2005; 
(b) if so, what are the special features of this scheme; 
(c) whether it will check the double taxation across the board; 
(d) what will be the benefits to th e common public through this VAT 
scheme; and 
(e) what will be the change in revenue collection if this process is 
implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM) (a) to (c) Value Added Tax is a State level tax 
reform measure which is proposed to be implemented by States in lieu of the 
existing Sales Tax system. The Central Government is playing the role of 
facilitator in this tax reform process.  VAT is a simple, transparent, multi-
stage tax with input tax credit, which e liminates cascading of taxes. Further, 
as decided by the Empowered Committ ee, it is expected that a number of 
State level taxes on purchase or sales of goods like State sales tax, turnover 
tax, purchase tax, additional sales tax, surcharge, entry tax (not in lieu of 
Octroi) will be sub-sumed in VAT. Henc e, instead of multiplicity of taxes, 
there would only be a single tax. 
(d) The provision of Input Tax Credit (ITC) is one of the most significant 
features of VAT which ensures that ther e is no cascading of tax (i.e.tax on 
tax) and no consequent price escalation which is ultimately beneficial to the 
common public. 
(e) International experience suggests that VAT is revenue enhancing. 
However, actual impact on revenues of States/UTs shall be known only after 
VAT is actually implemented by the States/UTs.

(c) Article 243G of the Constitution prov ides that the Legislature of the 
State may, by law, endow the Panchayats with such powers and authority as 
may be necessary to enable them to function as institutions of self-
government and such law may contain provisions for the devolution of

Panchayati Raj is mandated to facilitate and secure implementation of
